Research into time series models has largely focused on models with parametric representations, where each model component is defined by a scalar parameter. However, recent studies have moved away from this limitation in favor of non-parametric representations that allow for separate learned functions for each component. Although these new models achieve great results in practice, they lack theoretical backing in the form of analysis regarding their theoretical performance. In response, this study aims to delve into theoretical aspects of a specific non-parametric linear regression model with white noise components. It initially establishes a finite sample bound in the setting of linear models and then compares the bounds between parametric and non-parametric representations. Subsequently, this study conducts numerical experiments to investigate the impact of model complexity on prediction risk in non-parametric representations.

Speech enhancement in a single microphone setup using deep learning has achieved the best results so far. This paper is a revised version of our previous work presented at the 28th European Signal Processing Conference in 2018. We used a deep learning framework called CB-DL, which uses attention mechanisms and can be trained with real-world data. We used the ASR corpus and the Corpus Chessy in our experiments. Our results showed significant improvements compared to traditional time-domain modeling. We also found that our model outperformed other similar approaches.

A recent study investigates the negative impact of mixing public health information with enticing content, using an example from a UK rock band's controversial live performance. The researchers surveyed students during their lessons and found that messages delivered after the show were less effective at preventingEbola transmission, particularly among younger individuals and those with stronger desires for the music presented. Follow-up tests further explored the underlying mechanisms and long-lasting effects of this phenomenon. The study cautions against combining vital information with distracting content in settings where it may reach the general population.

We examine a scenario where an autonomous agent participates in a decentralized market and chooses how much energy to store for later use. Given the decision-making process is made with limited information and a cautious approach, it aims to minimize losses rather than maximize gains. A key feature of this research is applying a loss function within the learning process. We enhance the learning algorithm by incorporating a maximin strategy, enabling the agent to learn optimal behavior even when the market conditions are constantly changing. Theoretical and experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, particularly in scenarios with fluctuating prices.

The study of electron interaction and light absorption/diffusion involves understanding many-body quantum systems.  Despite advances, electron correlation processes that occur as electrons emit virtual photons remains a research gap.  Here, we investigate these interactions by examining the time-scale of the Auger-Meitner decay in xenon, which involves simultaneous emission of a photon and electron from an excited 3d shell.  Data was collected at a xenon filled free-electron laser beamline by analyzing xenon ions in a storage ring.  We found that the scale of electron-electron interaction can be inferred by comparing two types of decay - traditional 3d-shell decay and the simultaneous 3d-shell decay and emitted photon.  Longer lifetimes of excited states caused by shorter wavelengths of incident photons holds potential for increasing data resolution and precision of interaction scale measurements.

A computer simulation was used to examine a simplistic, globally rotating planet under various conditions of atmospheric rotation. These simulations were conducted using an overly simplistic model and tested at different ranges of a key factor, which influenced the planet's atmospheric rotation. The results showed distinct circulation patterns in these simulated worlds. In particularly rapidly rotating planets, thin bands formed across the planet, aligned with its axis of rotation. In slower rotating planets, the circulation was more chaotic, resembling eddies. Medium-speed planets exhibited different circulation patterns, aligned with the planet's axis of rotation. The orientation of these patterns was explained using two competing forces, which influenced the stability of these patterns. The simulated planets' patterns were compared to those used to explain patterns seen in gas giants like Jupiter. The results provided insights that could be applied to understanding the atmospheres of exoplanets.

Deep learning models have been successfully applied to diverse fields, including natural language processing and computer vision. Most of the successful implementations rely on static neural network training and periodic relearning with enhanced data. In contrast, less known is how images are processed by the vast number of people who use online photo repositories and visual search engines every day. To bridge this knowledge gap, we investigated the potential for continuous learning on a large scale. However, retraining from scratch is not always feasible due to the ever-changing nature of publicly available training data. Moreover, algorithms for continuous learning on a large scale have not been thoroughly tested. In response, we developed a framework to test such algorithms by creating a clean image dataset and one that reflects the dynamic properties of public training data. Our results demonstrate the potential of our framework and show that our proposed approach outperforms existing methods in simulated dynamic scenarios and real-world applications involving large datasets like Instagram and ImageNet. Our findings also highlight the challenges associated with modeling human learning from images, including the impact of low-quality annotations, low-resolution images, and diverse labeling styles. Our work paves the way for machines to learn from images in a continuous and unbounded manner. Source code is accessible online at https://github.com/facebookresearch/dynamic-cls.

This study provides novel analytical and geometrical insights into the complex algebraic multiplicity of isolated singular points of holomorphic maps from $N$ to $N$, encompassing both non-degenerate and degenerate cases. We derive an exclusive formula for the algebraic multiplicity of a map $f$ that combines several components, including contributions from the Lefschetz number of the normalized tangent map at a singularity, specific algebraic invariants of normalized power series, and geometric multiplicity of certain degenerate singular points. This combination of approaches enables calculation of the algebraic multiplicity for a broad spectrum of power series, encompassing those with non-trivial initial behavior and specific singularities like ordinary double points. These theories find practical applications in analyzing the algebraic multiplicity of singular points in plane and spatial curves and surfaces defined by implicit equations.

Our analysis examines how dipoles interact with an electromagnetic cavity under the optical phase assessment conditions, using a resonant configuration. Under these conditions, we analyze non-classical state generation, observing significant long-lived correlations in the dipoles due to a balanced interplay between Rabi coupling and decay. This allows for efficient collective optical phase estimation, with the dipoles in a coupled system creating the optimal state when the decay rates and coupling reach a critical ratio. Interestingly, our findings also reveal the emergence of squeezing in both normal and unusual forms. The highly entangled Gaussian wave function can be approximated by applying a quadratic interaction Hamiltonian. The proposed model offers insights into the complex dynamics of coupled quantum systems and offers potential value for phase assessment in the future.

Research into the development of quantum computers has focused on finding "natural qubits," and silicon-based donor electrons have been a prominent candidate, and in previous studies, we examined a system with four donor electrons and explored their exchange interactions and how they are influenced by valley splitting and host crystal symmetry, and our calculations utilized a modified effective mass model to account for multiple valleys and the coupling between them and allowed us to utilize well-known analytical expressions for the effective mass dispersion and this was complemented by atomic-scale first principles simulations and it enabled us to verify the accuracy of our effective mass model and provide corrections to previously assumed parameters, and our results showed that two strongly coupled electrons could reside in the same valley due to Pauli exclusion and the absence of exchange splitting when considering valley degrees of freedom, and the same was observed for three electrons, and our study yielded accurate predictions for the tetrahedral arrangement of four electrons that matched experimental observations and it showed nearly complete splitting between states and may implicate new methods for preparing qubit states and the corrections made to valley splitting and RPC in this study are critical in understanding the behavior of systems with multiple electrons and they should be incorporated into the design of registers based on donor-based quantum computers.

Researchers investigated the quantum conduction of HgTe quantum well thin films, searching for a connection between the absence of a band gap and conductive properties related to Dirac particles. Experimental data collected at a temperature of 0.3K and with a magnetic field of 10T revealed an interference pattern known as SHI in high-quality samples, indicating that large energy gaps created by adjusting hydrogen te parameters actually result in the quantum conduction of that energy gap. Furthermore, HQTs with specific delta-sublayer compositions showed quantum conduction related to Dirac electrons even in samples with completely closed energy gaps.

Machine learning-based cooperative NOMA technology in 5G intelligent transportation systems is promising yet resource-intensive, necessitating efficient and capable implementations. This research evaluates a path-based machine learning approach using a Cox proportional hazards model, where cooperative vehicles exchange and combine data to create virtual sensors through signal processing. By utilizing exchanged information, the cooperative sensors can more accurately identify obstacles, allowing for enhanced safety margins and improved performance. Furthermore, this study examines the Cox model's capability in various scenarios, including changing road conditions, varying speeds, and different safety margins, ultimately showing that a collaborative adaptive NOMA system outperforms traditional non-cooperative methods in intersection crossings.

This paper proposes a novel Game-Theoretic Framework for scheduling Dynamic TDD in five-generation networks. In this framework, each cell decides its own TDD configuration to improve reverse link throughput while considering the actions of neighboring cells. Due to the influence of interference, it is unlikely that an optimal scheduling solution can be achieved. However, the cell with the weakest signal strength from its neighbor has limited options for the TDD configuration and can anticipate the actions of neighboring cells. This allows for a cell to predict the actions of neighboring cells and choose the most beneficial TDD configuration. Simulations demonstrate that this framework significantly improves reverse link throughput by allowing cells to schedule their own transmission patterns.

A detailed analysis of the Hall resistivity of BSCCO thin films reveals that the Hall coefficient calculated from the carrier density derived from the peak positions of the vortex liquid phase does not align with the directly measured carrier density. This study examines the factors influencing this apparent discrepancy, and suggests that the difference arises due to the presence of empty sites within the copper-oxygen planes. A formula is derived to quantify this discrepancy, and its predicted outcomes are consistent with the observed carrier density data of the vortex liquid phase. Furthermore, the study derives the liquid phase pseudogap energy gap, and finds its magnitude to be approximately 15 meV, which matches the experimentally observed energy gap of approximately 12 to 18 meV.

Researchers have investigated high-order correlations in the 3D Ising model, specifically focusing on how they evolve with temperature near the critical point. A key observation made in this study is that certain differences between temperatures result in cumulative measurements that display a temperature-reversal symmetry. These specific differences are referred to as 'cumulants'. Further examination of these cumulants has revealed that at a particular temperature, called the 'fixed point temperature', they exchange values. Researchers have also found that these temperatures and the associated temperatures at which the system displays universal behavior can be accurately predicted using the renormalization group equations. Moreover, by applying an extrapolation technique, they have now obtained a more precise estimation for the Ising correlation length exponent. This new estimate has a significantly lower margin of error, standing at just 0.293(4), which surpasses the accuracy of previous measurements.

We introduce a family of irreducible commuting diagrams consisting of four large matrix algebras over the field of complex numbers, where each algebra is defined as a specific subalgebra of another algebra constructed using four integer parameters. Each building block algebra can be characterized by two of these integer parameters and acts as a subalgebra of another algebra constructed with different parameters. Instances where one algebra contains another are identified, allowing us to generate numerous examples of subfactor algebras with commuting squares. The representation types of these four algebras are fully reducible when they share a common direct summand in their decomposition matrices. The representation types of two pairs of these algebras are explored through the analysis of their modular representations. The algebras in question are shown to be closely related to algebras that generate the T_22 and T_23 families of commuting squares subfactor algebras.

In this work, we evaluate whether Hamiltonian Neural Networks can effectively acquire the capability of extracting useful gradients. Our primary tool for this evaluation is the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method. Although the HMC method relies on simulating Hamiltonian dynamics, recent research has revealed that neural networks trained as Hamiltonians can be overfit with fewer parameters than traditional architectures. Furthermore, these networks exhibit a notable efficiency in memory usage during training. Despite these advantages, it remains unclear whether the gradients produced by these networks meet the required standards. To address this question, we conducted a series of experiments across multiple datasets and tasks, yielding negative results. Specifically, we found that the HMC method is either ineffective or significantly less effective when employing OHAs powered by OHNs, in contrast to the established superiority of SBMC over SBMC. These findings have significant implications when considering larger batch sizes, a frequent requirement in machine learning tasks.

Deep learning systems can be deceptive and misleading, which is why developing approaches that genuinely convey true information becomes crucial. One method that has gained popularity is called "data-driven interpretability," utilizing existing or newly created, related data to train auxiliary models that provide reliable explanations for primary models. These auxiliary models can generate accurate interpretations for individual instances, but their models are still limited in providing explanations for multiple agents. In this study, we propose a novel approach that involves two auxiliary models working in coordination to offer credible explanations for a limited number of agents who are evaluating a primary model. The primary model's response to a new data point is compared to the predictions made by the auxiliary models on a similar, previously collected dataset. Consequently, the primary model's model is not altered, but the explanation is expanded by generating additional, related data points based on the auxiliary models' predictions, which are then gathered with the human agent's input. We tested our approach on several data sets and found that it outperformed a baseline method.

In security inspections, recognizing prohibited items in luggage contains an overwhelming number of small, camouflaged objects set against a complex background, which can elude detection even in secure examination X-ray images. Deep learning techniques have shown promise in this area, but a lack of comprehensive research limits their progress. To bridge this gap, our study presents one of the first extensive investigations into X-ray security inspection, comprising a new high-standard benchmark with over one million diverse backgrounds and more than ten categories of prohibited items. To enhance the security inspection performance, our proposed Lateral Inhibition Module (LIM) effectively mimics the security inspection X-ray device's inherent ability to identify objects by minimizing interference between adjacent areas in the image. To our knowledge, this is the first instance of introducing a lateral inhibition-inspired module in the field of X-ray security inspection using deep learning. Our experiments demonstrate that integrating LIM with state-of-the-art deep learning models yields a significant improvement of at least 5% accuracy. Furthermore, our high-standard benchmark and source code are publicly accessible at https://github.com/cjy2017/OneMillionXrayLIM.

We introduce a new polynomial invariant for links in $T^2 \times I$ that is based on path expansions and satisfies a specific splitting rule. This invariant behaves similarly to volume theories seen in Topological Quantum Computation and statistical mechanics models like the 3D Potts model and dimer models. By comparing our new invariant to the standard Torres relation, we derive an upper bound for its magnitude that relates to linking length.

The relative rarity of multi-word entries in annotated corpora hinders the
development of Word Sense Discriminatory capabilities. To overcome this
constraint, we propose an innovative approach that leverages additional
information by replacing each word within a context with a descriptive gloss
that specifies the word's basic meaning. This enables a comparison between
multi-word entries and single-word words by equating the extent of their
respective contextual information and their semantic information. We
demonstrate the efficacy of this proposed approach by significantly
outperforming alternative methods in a sense selection task, particularly
when dealing with multi-word entries. Furthermore, research findings
indicate that models performing well in this task are highly sensitive to
wording of the provided contexts and the included glosses. Additionally,
they are susceptible to the priming effect of the changes made to the
semantics of the entries and the surrounding contexts. To address these
limitations and gain deeper insights, we propose four strategic approaches
to refine the retrieval of semantic and background information: namely,
expanding the word context to a multi-word entry context, controlling the
coherence of the retrieved word contexts, expanding the descriptive scope
of the included glosss, and utilizing more precise semantic control.

This study defines a novel class of Hilbert space functions, denoted as K_alpha, and proves that the normalized reciprocal Gamma function, y_al, belongs to K_al for all non-negative real numbers 'a'. We also demonstrate that y_al is the minimal element of K_alpha for all such 'a'. Furthermore, our novel approach to representing y_al through integral and series expansions is proven to be the most efficient using the K_alpha class criteria.

Research into the top quark generation mechanism, specifically involving a single photon and gluon, is initiated to assess the significance of these processes. Considerations of additional processes such as electroweak boson emission are included in this examination. Using realistic detector settings, we present predictions for experimental outcomes at the Large Ion Collider and examine how these processes compare to the dominant gluon-initiated process.

Effectively solving the cross-domain text-to-SQL task is highly dependent on a proper linguistic analysis, particularly in generating an accurate hierarchical schema. To achieve this, a comprehensive end-to-end model for cross-domain text-to-SQL has been developed, which focuses on three key subtasks: embedding generation, link prediction, and label creation. The model utilizes specialized submodels for each subtask and a unique auxiliary task-based transformer to manage the high dimensionality of the output schema space. An open-source framework has been created, offering pre-trained submodels, to facilitate the preparation of data for the current and future text-to-SQL challenges.

The rising reliance of individuals and organizations on social networks and the subsequent need to safeguard personal privacy have sparked considerable research into differential privacy (DP) applied to graph data. This DP variant, characterized by limiting access to sensitive information within graphs to protect individual privacy, has seen numerous applications in analysis and learning tasks involving graph data. As interest in this area expands, a variety of DP-protected graph learning techniques have emerged. Nevertheless, a comprehensive understanding of the field is yet to be achieved due to rapid development and isolated study approaches. This research study aims to address these gaps by providing a thorough exploration of the DP secrecy differential on graphs, covering topics such as basic DP theory on graph data, DP-preserving graph learning applications and enhancements, and potential future research directions. Furthermore, it proposes a taxonomy to categorize current and future DP-protected graph learning techniques based on their underlying models and learning algorithms.

The upcoming launch of the Euclid satellite in 2022 will significantly advance our understanding of the universe's geometry and content, as well as the potential for discovering new phenomena beyond the visible spectrum. The Euclid mission, comprising a sophisticated camera and spectroscope, is designed to gather a vast amount of data through weak gravitational lensing, supernovae measurement and redshift mapping. This will result in the exploration of the standard model of cosmology with greater precision, while also offering the opportunity to discover new physics beyond it. The Euclid inheritance science opportunities report outlines the key questions and scientific capabilities that the mission will tackle, as well as the need for the Euclid community to define the data formats and processing methods that the satellite will use. This will ensure the efficient extraction of scientific insights from the massive amount of data that the Euclid satellite will collect over the course of the mission.

To effectively test autonomous lane-changing systems, a specialized network of difficult paths is typically created by generating complex road layouts with a variety of features, such as the optimal path is created by a method that iteratively adjusts a starting and ending point to create a new path and evaluates it with an optimization algorithm until a better path is found.

However, the process of creating benchmark paths can be time-consuming and laborious when done manually, which limits its effectiveness. To address this issue, a more efficient method is proposed that leverages a mathematical formula to create interconnected paths within a larger network, providing a scalable and versatile testing environment for autonomous vehicles.

The proposed method involves using a probabilistic approach to adjust the parameters of the created paths to either add connectivity to the network or create isolated components, allowing for a highly connected network of paths that can challenge an autonomous vehicle's navigation system. The proposed method is shown to be effective in creating complex networks of paths that an autonomous vehicle's lane-changing system is unable to navigate from start to finish, shattering the vehicle's claimed ability to do so.

The proposed method is also shown to be versatile, as it can be used to create highly connected networks of paths that an autonomous vehicle's navigation system is unable to navigate from start to finish, as well as isolated components that can test the vehicle's ability to navigate in a variety of scenarios. The proposed method is also used to create novel benchmark paths that can be used to test the autonomous vehicle's navigation system

The organization of music playlists into descriptive categories aids users in quickly finding what they're looking for. While some music streaming services already allow for categorized music, there's still room for improvement in providing concise summary titles for a larger proportion of playlists. Our proposed approach aims to provide concise summary titles for music playlists by utilizing sequential music annotation techniques. Initially, we convert the lists of songs and associated metadata into detailed descriptive statements. These statements are then labeled with corresponding temporal positions. Finally, we utilize sequential annotation tools to generate concise summary titles that capture the essence of the playlists. Our proposed methodology is evaluated through comprehensive experiments and user studies, demonstrating the effectiveness of the generated music summary data and the proposed approach in organizing music lists for enhanced artificial intelligence processing.

A new hydrodynamic theory called the Phase-space Random Quantum Hydrodynamics (PRQH) has been developed to describe the collective behavior of a two-component bosonic fluid. This theory builds upon the established Random Quantum Hydrodynamics (RQH) framework and incorporates Heisenberg's uncertainty principle into the equations of hydrodynamics. As a result, PRQH offers enhanced accuracy in predicting the dynamics of low-density fluids while maintaining applicability across all density regimes. PRQH shows that the quantum Bohm-Peierls effect plays a crucial role in fluid behavior even at high densities and can be experimentally observed. Furthermore, PRQH was applied to investigate the mixing and sound mode damping processes in identical particles and can be extended to include particles with different masses, sizes, and interaction strengths.

Temporal action recognition in video brings unique challenges due to extensive variations in action timing and wealth of context present in the scene. A prominent Network of Contextual Decoders (NCC) has previously been proposed, which is capable of capturing dual context (semantic and spatial) and integrating it across different time points. NCC's framework comprises a series of separate contextual analysis modules (DCAs), but such an arrangement risks becoming mired in excessive model complexity and lack of flexibility. In an effort to streamline the NCC structure, this paper presents a refined DCAn element that incorporates all contextual context extraction modules (global pooling, bidirectional feature extraction, bidirectional attention mechanism, and NFA) into a unified design. Each DCAn takes only a direction of context and integrates it with temporal information at a distinct stage. Due to its modular nature, DCAn can be readily adapted across different backbones, enabling a more efficient context exploitation and performance boost in temporal action recognition. Due to its ability to effectively extract and integrate the scene context present, the proposed DCAn structure endows video actions with a deeper understanding, resulting in significant accuracy improvements in temporal action recognition.

The long-lived JET palm tree modes (PTLs) have recently been studied with careful analysis of available data from previous experiments. A significant difference between the current PTLs and other historical events, such as the Torsional Alfv\'en Modes in JT-60 or the Pseudo-PTLs in DIII-D, lies in their distinct relationship with edge localized modes (ELMs). The new data does not support the earlier belief that PTLs act as a barrier against the buildup of pressure at the edge of the plasma. Instead, the previous events and the JET PTLs should be considered separate phenomena. The absence of rotation shear in the central plasma during JET PTLs distinguishes them from other similar events. The trigger mechanism behind PTLs appears to be the magnetic field line erosion of the plasma edge. As for the nature of PTLs, they likely result from an interaction between the Palmer instability and the resistive tearing mode. To move forward, future experiments should focus on increasing the plasma pressure gradient and rotation shear near the edge to either stimulate or inhibit the occurrence of PTLs.

This research focuses on addressing collision avoidance and collision-free navigation in a 2D plane for a team of mobile robots with a simple control scheme called the Dynamic Vortex Potential, which is both collaborative and takes into account future positions of the robots to prevent collisions. We demonstrate that for any number of robots in any initial configuration, the simple DLVP achieves smooth, collision-free movement and convergent behavior at attractive points, all without requiring communication between the robots. Furthermore, for scenarios with limited visibility range, we prove that the simple DLVP also ensures collision-free operation, which was further verified through numerical examples and a real-world experimental test using a physical robot.

The human brain is wired for processing words made up of sequences of sounds and symbols, yet the neural mechanisms for recognizing sequences have been less studied compared to pattern recognition. Researchers have utilized letter combinations from the English alphabet in experiments because they are easy to manipulate artificially, despite having little meaning. A novel experimental setup was used to gather independent samples of letters from various sequences, from random strings to meaningful words, and sentences. The results showed that independent samples of letters from meaningful words and sentences significantly deviated from the expected average frequency of each letter in accordance with Sanov's theorem, while deviations were one normal deviation away for random strings. These findings were verified using simulated data with independent samples drawn from matrices generated through the Levy distribution. The study also explored the concept of relative entropy in both additive and multiplicative forms, as well as its applications in neuroscience and economics.

The rapid adoption of Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS) has sparked our investigation into their potential advantages for radar systems, specifically in the context of target parameter estimation. Through the mathematical modeling of a passive IRS-assisted radar system, we have developed an equation that describes target parameter estimation accuracy. This model allows us to analyze how the interaction between direct and IRS-assisted radar and target signals is affected by various variables, including the number of direct and IRS-assisted receiver and target antennas, the size of the IRS, and their relative positioning. The resulting insights reveal that, unlike traditional radar systems, IRS-assisted radar systems can significantly enhance target parameter estimation accuracy through strategic deployment of the IRS. Leveracing the reflective capabilities of the IRS, our work provides a design approach for surface units that can achieve superior estimation performance, as theoretically proven through numerical simulations.

Discovering vulnerabilities in a target application using a fuzzer is a time-consuming and often impractical process of waiting for it to succeed. Due to the low efficiency of traditional fuzzing, accurately predicting the success of such an endeavor and assessing the efficiency of the fuzzer before it completes the task is actually more challenging than the task itself. Unfortunately, most existing evaluation metrics are simply based on the performance indicators provided by the fuzzing tool itself and are prone to deception. In contrast, this paper introduces a set of non-self-reported evaluation metrics for in-process evaluation, along with methods to assess the velocity and potential of discovered anomalies. Through the establishment of a customized fuzzing platform and an extensive evaluation of nine widely-used fuzzers, this paper demonstrates the limitations of existing metrics and highlights the superiority of the proposed metrics through comparative experiments.

Our analysis reveals that integrating a pretrained model in continual learning frequently leads to subpar results compared to a basic baseline, which employs a simple averaging strategy for loss computation. We further observe that the beneficial impact of the pretrained network's knowledge is not consistent, but heavily relies on the specific task features. As a result, significant improvements, notably up to 15% greater accuracy, can be achieved by using the straightforward baseline in continual learning scenarios.

We establish a foundational framework for variational calculus on surfaces that minimize distances within specified homotopy paths in metric spaces. This framework includes definitions for weak and limited derivatives, as well as first-order conditions for critical surfaces. The concept of minimal surfaces is further developed, and it is demonstrated that limited derivatives exist everywhere on optimal surfaces, thus ensuring they are critical. A specific example is provided, showing that in $\mathbb{R}^3$, a minimal homotopy-one-connected surface can still exhibit the behavior of hanging strips.

This final installment concludes our comprehensive survey of long-term solution behaviors for solutions of the heat equation on the real line. These solutions can be obtained from initially bounded data, and we've categorized data at given times into three distinct classes based on their decay rates. Initially data whose solutions exhibit specific time dynamics can be manipulated and transformed. We examine and illustrate the connections between these three categories, and the behavior of solutions for all three, including previously unexplored cases, by means of both theoretical and numerical means. This work builds on the research presented in the two preceding volumes.

Recent research has identified an unusual, stable state in the 64Ni nucleus, where two different configurations with the same energy and spin exist simultaneously. In a theoretical analysis, we found that a delicate interplay between two forces - surface and tensor interactions - is likely maintaining this rare phenomenon. By fine-tuning the balance between these competing forces, we anticipate 64Ni to exhibit similar form coexistence in neighboring isotopes, particularly in 62, 64, and 68Ni. Our study aims to provide a foundational understanding of this novel concept, forming the basis for more precise predictions regarding these related nuclei.

Lipschitz query games are a type of mechanism design where the objective is to determine the minimum query complexity of an equilibrium that can be achieved by answering yes/no questions. This equilibrium can then be used to classify inputs into two categories. Recent breakthroughs have revealed the existence of equilibria with low query complexity ($O(\sqrt{n})$) and those with specific properties, such as being formed by questions that partition the input space into two equal halves. However, existing lower bounds for the query complexity of equilibria are relatively high, being confined to the $O(n^{0.62})$ bound. This research aims to improve this bound to $O(n^{0.575})$.

Machine learning model tuning through evaluation metrics typically employs a train-test split or cross-validation technique to optimize performance. However, due to random sampling, especially with smaller datasets, it is common for significantly varying results to occur when running the process multiple times. This inconsistency ultimately leads to unreliable average outcomes that do not accurately reflect the true performance potential of a given NLP model. Our novel approach, utilizing the J-K fold cross-validation technique, aims to enhance the reliability of E-by-average results for NLP model tuning by addressing this issue. This method involves dividing both training and testing datasets into K folds, then sequentially training on combinations of the K folds and evaluating them against the remaining fold, ultimately leading to a significant reduction in variance of the results (p < 0.05). As demonstrated in our case study on a sentiment analysis task, our approach yields a substantial decrease in the gap between the best and average outcome (from 20% to 5%), thereby providing a more accurate representation of a model's true performance potential.

The concept of multivariate knowledge representation has long been the focus of extensive research in the field of Artificial Intelligence. Despite numerous studies in this area, existing surveys on the topic do not adequately consider the educational aspect of generated knowledge. To address this limitation, the KGE community has made significant headway in developing learned representations that facilitate human-pupil and multivariate relationship understanding. Given the analogous nature of educator-pupil and pupil-youngster frameworks, this review examines the literature in preparation for the application of Knowledge Graphs as a tool for effective knowledge transfer and learning by the educator-pupil framework. By combining the educator-pupil and pupil-youngster frameworks, it is hypothesized that an integrated system will be capable of acquiring both human-understandable knowledge and knowledge that leads to successful task performance.

The global maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation in a Markov random field (MRF) is mathematically equivalent to solving a constrained optimization problem. Due to the exponential increase in possible label combinations in an MRF, brute force methods are impractical for solving this problem exactly, especially as the number of variables and potential labels grows rapidly. One efficient approach to address this issue is the sum-product method, which can be effective for smaller systems but fails to account for other high-a posteriori labels when there are multiple variables involved, thus always producing sub-optimal results. Other methods, such as Lagrangian optimization, have been proposed to provide a faster maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation, yet they often result in non-linear equation systems that are extremely difficult to solve exactly. In this research, a novel exact maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation method is introduced, utilizing an expanded function form to quickly determine the Lagrangian function's optimum value within minutes, outperforming the sum-product method and existing constrained optimization techniques by a significant margin.

In the high-resolution search for fundamental violations of nature's laws, scientists use cold atom systems as reference frames and try to minimize errors by precisely measuring optical transition frequencies. Typically, experiments with cold atoms involve multiple beams to cool and detect atoms, which can create complexities due to the different beams interacting in various ways. Researchers have developed novel techniques to create extremely cold clouds of strontium atoms using only a single laser beam, achieving temperatures as low as 28 micro-Kelvin. In this study, they carefully examined the impact of the photon recoil from the laser beam on rubidium atoms, discovering that it causes a shift in the 5s to 6p transition frequency, which decreases as the laser intensity increases and is more significant at higher temperatures. This discovery indicates that a single-beam experiment provides a cleaner platform for such violations searches, while also showing that previous experiments using a single beam have possibly already detected the influence of this phenomenon on frequency measurements based on the atoms' velocity distribution and the Lorentzian line shape.

The sudden shift from shear thinning to shear thickening under a critical shear rate is a key feature of shear thickening fluids. This research seeks to identify the universal aspects of the transition by comparing the shear rate and stress behaviors before and after the critical point. Our findings show that, when normalized by their values at the critical point, the shear rate and stress exhibit a common pattern, indicating that the maximum stress reached during the shear thinning phase is proportional to the stress during the shear thickening phase. This proportionality holds across various concentrations of the fluid and can be explained through the free volume model, which suggests that the critical shear rate is directly related to the stress during the shear thinning phase.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra. This $sR(n)$ is then identified with a specific, special centralizer, known as the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, of a diagonal element within the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)^{\otimes n}$. The centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is then shown to be expressible as a tensor product of Virasoro algebras and its special subalgebras, known as $W^{(r)}$ algebras, for various values of $r$, for a sufficiently high value. This relationship allows a high rank Racah algebra $R(n)$ to be described as a collection of Virasoro algebras or $W^{(r)}$ algebras, and consequently, $sR(n)$ can be viewed as semi-direct sums of these algebras and their universal enveloping spaces, and it allows calculation of the Hilbert-Poincaré series and coefficients thereof.

Our analysis indicates that within a certain range of conditions, fluid magnets exhibiting a honeycomb structure and based on a triplon system can experience distinct phases, including supersolid and superfluid states. Specifically, in an elongated oblate shape, an order parameter capable of maintaining rotational symmetry in two dimensions can give rise to a solid-like magnetic phase. Utilizing a dimer-triplon expansion approach, our study aims to investigate the triplon phase structure near the SO(3)-symmetry breaking point in various curved geometries. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that certain curved geometries for bilayer honeycomb magnets can support both the dimer and triplon orders equally, allowing for an efficient description of multiple order components through Ginzburg-Landau theory. Consequently, our theory predicts the existence of exotic curved supersolid and superfluid phases for triplons in certain curved magnets, a prediction that may be tested experimentally via inelastic neutron scattering.

This study examines the correlation between incident speed and recoil angle in WIMP-nucleus scattering, relying on three-dimensional simulations. Our findings indicate that, in contrast to two-dimensional scenarios where this correlation holds strongly due to dominant forward scattering, the correlation is considerably weaker in three-dimensional space. Furthermore, when narrowing the angle of interest, the effective incident speed distribution exhibits a noticeable shift towards lower speeds. This effect becomes increasingly pronounced as the nucleon number of the target target increases, owing to the narrower recoil energy spectrum found in heavier targets. Consequentially, incorporating speed-dependent effective parameters into machine learning-based WIMP searches is essential for accurately assessing such events.

The extent of information on the World Wide Web exceeds human capacity to fully process, raising the importance of web search as a means to filter out unnecessary content. One key concern is whether Google's personalization, which tailors search results to the user, influences the filtering process. To examine this, the research team designed a controlled experiment with participants using Google Web search for the lowest-stakes decision available, namely choosing between chocolate and cheese. The results revealed that non-personalized searches led to less bias than their personalized counterparts. Furthermore, the data indicated that as few as 20 top search results are typically viewed, with the influence of the few highly-ranked pages above it diminishing rapidly. The research team modeled this effect and discovered that, due to Google's personalization, users often miss out on relevant information about their preferences present on the Web and instead allow the content of the few highly-ranked pages to overemphasize their desires.

Proposed projects, including an electron-ion and muon-nucleus collider, could
leverage the Muon-Nucleon Synchrotron at Fermilabe, effectively utilizing
existing infrastructure and capabilities of Muon Synchrotron at Fermilabe.  By
combining this with high-energy electron beams from an advanced electron
synchrotron, researchers can utilize deeply virtual Compton scattering and deeply
inelastic scattering for precision electron data that can guide and calibrate
hadron data, reducing uncertainties in parton distribution functions.  This
will enable cleaner interpretation of proton data and lead to more precise
determination of the physics of heavy quarks, lepton universality, and CKM
angle phasing.  Furthermore, these processes can reveal the origin of matter
and antimatter asymmetry in b-quark decay.  The facility will also facilitate
irreversible proton scattering, offering unprecedented sensitivity in searching
for new physics beyond the Standard Model, potentially as direct or indirectly
at energy scales up to 9 TeV.

Traditional respiratory motion correction methods struggle with traditional 2D or 3D T2-weighted (T2w) MRI due to their short TR timing, causing distorted images affected by respiratory motion. Researchers have utilized this technique to create a four-dimensional (4D) MRI, accounting for the three spatial dimensions and temporal component. They employed a multi-shot, free-breathing T2w MRI in four dimensions, utilizing a reversed phase - rephased phase encoding strategy to create motion - corrected high-resolution images free of distortion affected by respiration. Researchers used this novel sequence to successfully scan the lower abdomen and lower extremities of healthy volunteers in a free-breathing state, accurately capturing the soft tissue and bone structures even near the skin. The success of this method was further highlighted by its ability to detect a tumor in a patient, showcasing its potential for high-quality motion - corrected MRI in four dimensions.

A key challenge in controlling dynamic systems is ensuring their outputs stay within predetermined safe limits during operation. Control barrier functions are a powerful tool used to address this challenge in non-stochastic environments. However, their effectiveness is limited when systems are subject to uncertain noise, as they cannot guarantee safety in such environments. In this paper, we expand the concept of control barrier functions to include a set of allowable control inputs. This novel framework, which we call an input-restricted control barrier function, enables the synthesis of controllers that keep system states within predefined safe limits while respecting the given control inputs. By leveraging IRCBFs, we can also design methods to synthesize controllers that not only maintain safety but also optimize certain performance criteria, taking into account the allowable control inputs. Finally, we explore how noise affects this new framework and develop an approach to ensure safety in noisy environments using modified input-restricted control barrier functions.

This paper reinterprets areas through the lens of CF-approximation spaces, leveraging known connections between rough sets and representation theory. Initially, we integrate basic concepts from rough set theory to set the stage for our primary argument. Subsequently, we apply this framework to establish that squared approximation spaces correspond to subobjects within a category of surjective homomorphisms, enabling us to utilize representation theory to analyze the rough sets category. This connection enables us to utilize vector space modules to investigate the rough sets category, which in turn aids in addressing the problem of computing its Klainerman-Taubes invariant. Our analysis also provides the necessary tools to address the area computation problem, exemplified by a solution to the problem of finding the area enclosed by the parametric curve defined by $\gamma(t) = (2t\cos(t) - 2\cos(t), 2t\sin(t) - 2\sin(t))$ for $t$ in the interval $[0, \pi/2]$.

Tests in paired situations are commonly analyzed using effect size metrics, which rely on data that has been rank-transformed and calculated on a per-person basis. The standard approach uses the Wilcoxon signed-rank test's test statistic. This method evaluates the distribution of a pre-determined function of differences between pairs of observations, which are the differences themselves in the case of the Wilcoxon test. While the existing research has successfully establish the paired permutations distribution (PPD) of effect size metrics under the null hypothesis as sample sizes increase, these studies used various methods, such as Monte Carlo simulations, recursive algorithms, or direct computation, to achieve their results. The approach taken in this research involves the use of paired permutations (PPT) scores to directly calculate the distribution of a given metric of effect size, regardless of the sample size. The results shown in the study confirm the accuracy of this approach, including its consistency with the PPD at smaller sample sizes, but also reveal a significant efficiency gain of up to 10-fold when comparing it to the traditional rank-based permutations (PPD) approach. The paper also explores the possibility of employing this approach in a live testing scenario, including the use of reference distributions to detect alterations in the underlying data, and demonstrates the accuracy of these distributions through an experimental approach. The study concludes by suggesting the use of more complex metrics in practical tests, and providing the open-source code used in the study's analyses.

The shipping industry is crucial to the global economy but lacks the comprehensiveness of a major economic data series due to the scarcity of consolidated shipping industry information over extended periods. This research addresses this gap by creating a extensive dataset covering freight rates, shipping volume, new vessel prices, used vessel prices, and scrapped vessel prices from 1966 to 2018. The dataset's completeness is demonstrated to be the result of a rigorous process of intensive cross-checking and validation. A unit root test on the dataset indicates that most variables are stationary in their level form. The Granger causality analysis and variance decomposition reveal a bidirectional supply and demand dynamic that characterizes the shipping market in the long run. The variable's impact on each other fluctuates over time in the short run. The results of the variable's on freight rates and the shipping volume exhibit persistence when vessel prices are considered in the short and long run. The study's significance is that it provides a comprehensive global shipping industry dataset over an extensive period of time.

We examine the properties of Marcumicchio fabrics, a type of triangulated space developed by filling a metric graph with a specific geometric pattern. By analyzing a modified version of this space, we determine its topological characteristics and provide a way to calculate its diameter. Our investigation also reveals how changes to the underlying graph affect the fabric's own topological features and those of its own underlying skeleton. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings in the context of evolving simplicial complexes.

Graph neural networks have become the go-to method for analyzing graphs, but their inner workings are often complex and opaque. Although some researchers have attempted to simplify their networks using post-hoc techniques, these are prone to inaccuracies. Our study introduces a different approach, a graph neural network framework that leads to natural simplicity within the network. By combining the Stunned Solver framework with the principles of the Natural Network framework, our method efficiently produces a streamlined and easy-to-understand network structure that maintains high accuracy. Unlike previous methods, our approach directly learns this simplified structure while maintaining competitiveness with state-of-the-post-hoc techniques in both performance and runtime.

The CountSketch algorithm is a straightforward method for approximating high-dimensional vectors and serves as the groundwork for several subsequent algorithms. Despite its apparent simplicity, the algorithm's effectiveness when facing adaptive adversaries remains relatively unexplored. We investigate this by examining sketch length 'k', and discover that against non-adaptive adversaries, CountSketch accurately estimates vectors of magnitude up to $2^{\Omega(k)}$. However, in contrast, when vectors can be adapted to the sketch, the estimatable magnitude drops significantly (by a factor of $4$) to $2^{0.25k + O(1)}$. Lastly, we present the concept of 'count-skinnable' distributions, for which the estimatable magnitude is restored to $2^{0.5k + O(1)}$.

This research builds upon the ideas from our previous study, combining techniques from geometric analysis and topology to decompose the scalar curvature of a locally conformally flat Riemannian manifold into four distinct components, given a 4-tuple of conformally related metrics. In our earlier work, we established this decomposition under specific singularity conditions at the boundary of a bounded domain. Now, assuming additional technical requirements and dropping the previous singularities condition, we aim to prove a revised conclusion that excludes the fourth component of the decomposition and seeks to determine the new, simplified conformal decomposition problem for scalar curvature.

A long-standing hypothesis in physics posited that liquid helium-4, in its normal state and when subjected to a magnetic field, would exhibit entropy generation through the diffusion of entropy-carrying vortices. This phenomenon could be manipulated by creating entangled vortex rings that could, upon recombination, result in the release of heat. However, recent experiments have revealed that the interaction between these vortices is dissipative, causing the rings to shrink and release heat, thereby contradicting the entropy generation hypothesis.

In this paper, the evolution of the entropy, viscosity, and the net charge within a collection of entangled vortex rings in liquid helium-4 is analyzed using principles of electromagnetohydrodynamics, taking into consideration both the resistive and frictionless nature of the interactions. Our findings suggest that the initial rapid changes in these parameters, within the context of He-4, would quickly give way to later, slower changes hearkening back to pure helical transformations occurring at larger time scales.

In a theoretical scenario involving charged vortices, it is shown that the net charge within the fluid would stabilize at values approaching a quantum analogous to the Bekenstein bound found in general relativity. This outcome holds the potential to provide fresh insights into the nature of fluid entropy and viscosity in the vicinity of black hole horizons.

One of the primary challenges in the fields of control and optimization is adapting to changing systems in real-time. Machine learning, in particular, has been proven effective in making predictions to support real-time decisions. When a control problem is formulated with an implicit prediction mechanism, such as a learned value function within a model-based reactive control framework, it becomes possible to examine its predictive capability. This, in turn, leads to the development of a secondary control problem aimed at enhancing the learning component's ability. Analyzing the connection between the primary and secondary control problems through the lens of the change-system adaptability theory enables the exploration of the real-time adaptive aspects. This, however, has limited application due to its representational constraints. Therefore, a secondary control problem is designed to capture the remaining flexible components, and the associated update rules are mapped back to the primary and primary+secondary problems, thus providing a more comprehensive understanding of the system's adaptive capabilities. The practical utility of this approach is demonstrated through the development of a predictive model control scheme and the utilization of nonlinear Gaussian processes for learning dynamic systems.

Using deep learning in deep neural networks has been the primary focus of many researchers due to its effectiveness in solving complex, nonlinear problems. As a cutting-edge model that combines artificial intelligence and natural language processing, BERT has been widely used for various tasks, including text classification and production. By leveraging pre-trained language transformers and feeding it vast amounts of labeled data, BERT creates an efficient model for multiple tasks. Specifically, we utilized the Shakespeare dataset to train BERT to predict stock prices and then improved its output using a generative adversarial network, which uses an untrained neural network to create highly realistic data by learning from an opponent that tests its authenticity. This combination of models enables more accurate predictions and generates plausible stock prices over time.

Recently, shared envelope formalism has shown significant potential in addressing top-quark decay processes, though it has also encountered issues with the interpretation of the time coordinate for specific particles. To mitigate this, we've developed a modified shared envelope formalism called SCATTER, which introduces an additional shared component known as the "envelope," thereby preventing the confusion arising from the same physical particle being both a decay product and a byproduct of another process. This additional component enables the shared envelope formalism to be applied to shared-particle processes beyond the scope of certain particle types, such as self-enclosed decay chains. We've demonstrated the efficacy of this approach by computing the scattering process involving two shared $t\bar{t}$ pairs with the envelope, which could be particularly useful in distinguishing signal events from background noise in future high-energy physics experiments.

This research investigates the production of two Higgs bosons at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with center-of-mass energies of 3 TeV and 1 TeV, respectively. The study focuses on detecting the characteristic effective field theory signatures that would result from these events through analyses of final state particles. Specifically, it highlights that certain decay chains, namely HHP S→ (γγ) (bb̄) and HHP S → (γγ) τ + τ −, offer clearer signals due to the presence of photon pairs in the final state. Through detailed simulations and background estimations, it demonstrates the potential of these channels to distinguish BSM interactions through signature separations with high confidence, particularly for the 3 TeV CLIC collider where a deviation of one standard deviation can be detected.

We examine the standard approaches to modeling classical general relativity by exploring their equivalent Lagrangian frameworks. This analysis involves exploring the gravitational Lagrangians based on the Palatini method and the Hilbert formulation, as well as exploring various alternatives to the Einstein-Hilbert integral, including the Maxwell-Cachazo-Ewals and the Verlinde-Etoku-Labastie integral. We highlight the distinct outcomes of each of these approaches when applied to both standard general relativity and f(R) gravity.

To examine the stability of strong shocks moving perpendicularly in a five-dimensional AdS space, we utilized a method to split complex, profile-moving shocks into simpler pieces and analyzed their response to a specific type of perturbation. This study revealed that the accuracy of this series analysis increases when the speed of the shocks decreases. Our method was also employed to explore the behavior of shocks moving at the speed of light. We found clear indications of an even-odd pattern in the series coefficients around an intermediate state, which our hypothesis suggests corresponds to a distinct localized shock that can exist independently within the AdS space.

We calculated the drag experienced by a long cylinder moving through a bed of sand that has been watered, considering various angles of movement. This study determined an effective speed at which the cylinder moves, taking into account the anisotropy of the drag it experiences. Our model showed the effective speed to be directly proportional to the square of the cylinder's length and inversely proportional to the product of sand's area, with an interesting parameter representing the anisotropy of the drag. This relationship was verified with both theoretical models using long cylinders and short cylindrical objects, as well as experimental results. Our findings also SHW revealed that for dry sand, the anisotropy of the drag is influenced by the angle at which the cylinder moves, the density of the sand, the viscosity of any fluid present, the diameter of the cylinder, and the size of the grains making up the sand. These relationships were expressed through clear mathematical formulas.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a starburst galaxy called NGC 5907, discovering a correlation between outflows and star formation across its disk. Our data revealed the outflows are driven by medium-sized atoms and molecules moving at speeds of about 40 to 60 km/s, creating a bubble within the galaxy's disk. The bubble effectively limits star formation by reducing the amount of gas available in the disk and balancing forces within it. As a result, most of the galaxy's star formation occurs in the inner regions where outflows are strong enough to form this bubble. Our findings suggest that outflows create a self-regulating mechanism for the galaxy, influencing its long-term evolution and potentially representing a common process in the history of disk galaxies.

We introduce Organized Bayesian Optimization from Records (BoGraph), a Bayesian optimization method that leverages records to efficiently determine optimal settings for complex systems with multiple parameters on computers, robots, or other devices that are costly to adjust. Organized Bayesian Optimization from Records builds a organized inference graph based on the records and infers the most effective settings by minimizing a complex, non-differentiable cost function. To illustrate its benefits, we compare BoGraph to other methods in a comprehensive experiment involving the settings of a computer's operating system in a web-crawling task. Results indicate that Organized Bayesian Optimization from Records outperforms the alternatives by marginally improving performance by at least 5% and reducing runtime by at least 10% in multiple instances.

Our research examined the connection between initial geometry and final momentum anisotropy by studying triangular flow $v_3$ in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions using the multiphase transport model. By normalizing the third-order moment of the event plane angle distribution to the amplitude of the third-order Fourier coefficient, we were able to compare our results to those from hydrodynamic calculations and ABMod. We found that while the absolute $v_3$ amplitude varies significantly with centrality, the normalized $v_3$ amplitude provides a more reliable and consistent centrality dependence. After accounting for the varying participation of initial particles based on the number of nucleon-nucleon collisions, the normalized $v_3$ amplitude in Au+Au collisions showed similar behavior for various degrees of centrality. Our results indicate that the normalized $v_3$ amplitude in Cu+Cu collisions, particularly in mid-central collisions, can accurately reproduce the corresponding results from Au+Au collisions under the assumption of initial energy density equilibrium.

The growth in size and diversity of web data has compromised its overall
quality, prompting the need for creating high-quality datasets for the web.
To address this challenge, researchers have proposed creating specialized subsets
of data that maintain specific structural properties, ensuring their suitability
for tasks such as indexing, search, and machine learning. Nevertheless, creating
and evaluating the quality of such datasets remains a manual and time-consuming
process. In response, we have developed QuAReS, a novel framework for defining
qualitative metrics for web resources and datasets, specifically focusing on
RDF data. By representing preferences as logical rules, our system not only
evaluates dataset quality but also scales to handle large datasets thanks to its
efficient OLAP storage structure. Furthermore, QuAReS allows for the automatic
generation of reports that include both numerical and visual representations of
qualitative assessments. By leveraging square-cube scaling in its OLAP structure,
our system can process substantial datasets, in our case, over 10GB of data,
therefor enabling reliable quality evaluation. By demonstrating its capability to
effectively measure dataset quality using a combination of statistical, structural,
and semantic criteria, our system not only addresses the challenge at hand but
also showcases its efficiency in handling large amounts of data.

When monitoring dynamic stochastic processes, continuous probability distributions are often used. From monitored data points, parameters of these distributions can be estimated by analyzing first and second moments, which are less sensitive to outliers and data noise. However, traditional methods like the method of moments may fail due to the discrete nature and irregularity of time series data. A new, effective technique is proposed for estimating the parameters of commonly used probability distributions (Normal, Gamma, Weibull, and Beta) based on their moments. The proposed method transforms raw observed values into binary sequences representing cumulative distribution values at observed time points, allowing the estimation of moments of a latent variable by aggregating recorded data and calculating quantile-based empirical cumulative distribution function values. The method is proven to be robust under theoretical analysis and simulations, ensuring the reliability of parameter estimates obtained through this method.

We used high-resolution spectra to analyze a Hα region in three active galactic nuclei at the periphery of their galaxies. This research extends our previous work on chemical compositions in Seyfert galaxies. We discovered that some emission lines, such as Hα, can show unusual patterns of electron density and metal abundance. Specifically, we found that the electron density in GH174730 was unusually high, while its metal abundance was normal. In GH103908 and NGC 1097, the electron density was typical, but their metal abundances were either extremely high or extremely low. We observed that linear gradients in metal abundance, commonly ionized by active galactic nuclei, can curve in unexpected ways. Furthermore, we discovered that post-shock plasma can create these unusual curvature patterns, suggesting that shock waves can create similar effects on plasma temperature and density. This creates new challenges for active galactic nuclei researchers, as it suggests that shock waves can create unusual chemical patterns that complicate their work.

Testing applications running on devices that need to adapt to changing device conditions is a challenging task due to the complex interactions between apps and their operating environments. Traditional testing methods struggle to manage this level of complexity, particularly in edge applications that must optimize for limited resources and varying device conditions. To address this issue, we have developed Event-Focused Testing, a novel approach for systematically testing applications in response to event-driven occurrences such as messages, notifications, and system logs. Event-Focused Testing generates test cases that simulate a wide range of events and their combinations, enabling more comprehensive application testing. Our results demonstrate that this approach is particularly effective for resource-constrained devices and can be applied to a variety of edge applications, including IoT systems and smart cities.

The ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has facilitated a range of investigations into phenomena involving beauty mesons, including studies on V^0 and rare decays, such as $B_s^0 \to mu^+ mu^-$ and mixed decays like $B^0 \to K^+ mu^- nu_e$ at LHCb, while also allowing for measurements of CP violation in the beauty system, such as those from light and flavor specific decays and from entangled $B^0_Bbar^0$ decays at LHCb. The ATLAS detector has contributed to improving the precision of form factor and branching fraction measurements for $B^0 \to * K^0$ and recorded an unprecedented amount of data for these investigations. Furthermore, with an expected increase in luminosity at the end of Run 3, the ATLAS detector is set to enter a period of refined and more comprehensive measurements and also data conditions that will significantly enhance the precision of form factor and branching fraction determinations and allow for the study of even rarer decays and CP violation in greater detail.

The current traffic models in real-to-virtual mapping technologies such as the autonomous vehicle testing are invaluable but lacking in realism. Realistic virtual traffic is complicated to achieve by manually designing each element due to the vast numbers of elements and real-world constraints involved. To overcome this difficulty, we propose an approach called SceneGen which utilizes machine learning to generate real-like traffic scenes by using actual traffic data. This is accomplished in two stages: an element generator creates plausible individual elements such as vehicles and road markings, while a scene regulator uses these elements to create real-like scene configurations. Both stages are trained using real traffic data without supervision or labeling. However, it is challenging to balance creativity and realism during generation. To mitigate this, we introduce guided elements and explicit constraints to real traffic scenes, enabling improved scene realism through experimentation. Our results show improved quality and realism of generated scenes compared to baseline models and various configured parameters.
On a Cayley tree, we prove the existence of new periodic Gibbs measures for the Ising model, which can be considered as analogues to Shaikhet's recently discovered mildly periodic Gibbs measures.

The choice of numerical method and discretization for a given PDE is guided by two primary considerations: guaranteed solution properties and computational efficiency. Modern scientific computation heavily relies on high-dimensional discretizations such as finite elements, finite differences, and difference schemes. These methods, while effective, often complicate the preservation of certain solution properties due to their artificial nature. Conversely, geometric discretizations directly translate continuous geometric and topological features into their discrete counterparts, thereby simplifying the challenge of maintaining desired solution properties. This paper delves into the role of preconditioning in relation to computational efficiency when using geometric discretizations like FOLG and mixed-formulations, particularly in the context of high-dimensional problems such as geodesic flows on manifolds. By replacing the expensive linear solves in a semi-explicit time-integration scheme with preconditioned Krylov methods, we investigate whether cheaper preconditioning can be combined with structure-preserving discretizations without compromising guaranteed solution properties. This inquiry involves both theoretical analysis and high-dimensional numerical experiments.

Let $f$ be a real-valued function and $h$ an integer sequence, both defined on the positive integers. We combine existing findings and introduce a new result to establish the ergodic independence and joint ergodicity of the sequence $f(n)$ and the integer sequence $h(n)$ along disjoint arithmetic progressions. Specifically, under certain conditions on $f$ and $h$, we prove the convergence $\lim_{N\to \infty} \frac{1_N\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{1_Q\sum_{j=1}^{Q}\frac{1_N\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}\big[\big(f(n)\bigr)\bigr]\bigr]\big(f(h(k+nj))\big)}{\varphi(N)\varphi(N+jQ)}}}{ to \mathbb{P}\big\{\big\{x\big\}\big\}\big\{x+h(nj)\big\}\big\}$, which holds significant number-theoretic implications and relies solely on the large-scale distribution properties of the sequences $f(n)$ and $h(n)$.

We investigated the formation of dust in low-metallicity environments, specifically in supernova-probed molecular clouds with metallicity 0.001 times the solar standard. Using 3D hydrodynamic simulations that accounted for temperature, density, and radiation changes due to Type II supernovae, we studied how dust grains form and evolve post-supernova. Our model dust particles were set at  iron/ nickel ratios, representing metallicity. The influence of radiation on these particles is significant until about 100 days post-supernova, after which they rapidly deplete the available silicon. As a result, we found that dust formation is more effective in environments 10 to 100 days post-supernova, where type II supernovae are likely to occur and the ambient molecular clouds are richest in coolant molecules. In these conditions, dust formation is so abundant that it significantly impacts the evolution of the supernova, causing it to shatter molecular clouds and expel them into space, potentially aiding in the widespread distribution of dust in the early universe and distant galaxies.

Detecting objects located several car lengths away in adverse weather conditions is a challenging task for autonomous vehicles. Current detection systems struggle in these scenarios due to limited point clouds, where three-dimensional detection performance significantly deteriorates. One major cause is the difficulty in distinguishing distant points due to noise in the sensor data. To address this issue, we have developed the Far3Det dataset, the first of its kind, featuring data on objects detected more than three vehicle lengths away in various and complex weather conditions. By experimenting with the Far3Det dataset, we have found the typical 3D detection accuracy to decrease heavily at distances beyond three car lengths, validating our approach. Additionally, we have performed extensive trials to explore methods of mitigating this decline, ultimately presenting the Far3DetBase model as a benchmark for future research and development in this field.

Proposing a method for generating estimated ground states of molecules through quantum machine learning, our approach involves a quantum parameterized model that approximates the ground state wavefunction, given the molecular Hamiltonian. - A classical non-iterative process is used to train this model's parameters, thereby offering an alternative to the commonly employed VQE algorithm. - The benefits of this method include avoiding local minima in the energy variation process and reducing the computational process into single classical iterations, which is particularly advantageous when using NISQ processors with inadequate classical communication capacity. - Although the method faces the challenge of Hamiltonian qubit restructuring during classical training, we can still achieve a efficient process when combined with fermionic operator theories, which preserve particle number. - The proposed method's feasibility is demonstrated with the help of a numerical simulation, which can be further validated with real-world molecular applications, namely H2, Li2, and Be2.

The Common Model for monkey brains is renowned for its comprehensive electrical annotation, covering nearly the entire brain, including within sulci, which has been accomplished using nearly 200 electrodes embedded in a flexible array. Despite the success of this approach in monkeys, directly applying a flexible electrode array to the human brain would pose safety concerns due to the numerous cracks in the cerebral cortex. This research explores the use of a novel, non-invasive volume-to-surface mapping technique that incorporates a data-informed biomechanical model to accurately predict brain deformation and create a high-resolution surface map of the underlying brain activity, even without direct measurements within the sulci. This technique was tested using realistic simulations and real MRI data, with the results showing that it can achieve a high degree of accuracy in predicting brain activity on the brain's surface even when using a limited number of electrodes. A comparative analysis with other methods also indicated that it can outperform the current industry standard for mapping the human brain's electrical activity non-invasively.

Conformal conservation of the energy-momentum tensor is investigated within conformally stationary, spherically symmetric spacetimes, and the conditions and equations for conformal Killing vectors are derived under this specific symmetry.

Guidance-based scene flow estimation models are highly efficient yet vulnerable to flawed target networks and misleading useful neighbors in the volume when processed in parallel. Adversarial metrics learning has the potential to resist such deception and enhance model performance by learning an optimal distance metric that balances accurate flow prediction and efficient computation.
