The results indicate the most plausible temperature range to be between 500-900 K, the most accurate radial velocity as -19.6 km/s, and the average abundance of elements in GJ 229B's atmosphere to be 0.27 times the solar standard. In particular, this study suggests the most likely temperature range for GJ 229B's atmosphere to be 550-750 K, which contradicts some previous studies but the discrepancy may be attributed to unmodeled atomic spectra or clouds within the dwarf's atmosphere. Further high-quality spectroscopic analysis is necessary to resolve this issue.

Using the quark-gluon transport model, we investigate the nature of profound inelastic scattering experienced by a test quark within a medium, and determine how its duration relates to spatial distance. Our findings demonstrate that, as the spatial distance increases, the interaction time decreases, and eventually becomes insufficient for the formation of inelastic scattering. Additionally, we discover over-damping behavior in the system's single-particle spectrum, and its direct correlation with the medium's viscosity.

Predicting how a scene will change and how the view will alter in the future is challenging because it requires a 3D understanding of the environment from imperfect 2D input. To prepare for future changes, models must handle a vast array of possible viewpoints, often exceeding 360 degrees, even when limited to rotating around a single axis. In this research, a novel approach is presented that combines two representation methods to tackle these complexities. This strategy involves initially simplifying the task of view transformation to a 3D rotation using a deep complex network, before tackling object occlusion in a second network. The result is an innovative framework for predicting how a scene may change, allowing for view transformations up to 180 degrees in increments of 15 degrees, even when only a single 2D image is available. Our model outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques on the widely-used KITTI benchmark, which has been made available with accompanying scene reconstructions and ground truth data for training and testing purposes. The proposed network also excels in generalizing to unseen objects, outperforming current methods on both the KITTI benchmark and a customized dataset, which has been particularly difficult due to the presence of a vast array of diverse objects, including many from unseen classes, in its sequence of images, which includes large disparities in object types, genres, and styles, as well as difficulties with low-resolution and compressed images, and lighting issues.

The behavior of electrons within interacting orbitals varies significantly,
with a key feature being the inter-orbital interaction.  This type of
electron-electron interaction is not commonly seen in its purest form in
any given material.  We present, with both theoretical and experimental
approaches, the detection of the distinctive signatures of the
inter-orbital interaction.  Our work involves applying a periodic
kinds of light to a particular material, resulting in isolated orbitals, and
observing their specific response.  The absence of electron spin entanglement
simpliciter enables the use of this technique as a sensitive indicator of
the desired interaction.  We have demonstrated that when the light applies
at right angles to each other, the material requires the activation of two
specific frequencies for resonance, while resonance is achieved at a single
frequency when the light applies in the same direction.  The observed
phenomena are explained using a theoretical model basing on the
Langevin equations.  The technique is demonstrated experimentally, utilizing
a doped insulator, Y3Fe5O12, and the resonance is clearly seen in the
reflective spectra.  This work paves the way for the application of ultrafast
spectoscopy to the investigation of the desired electron-electron
interaction in multiple materials.

The Ω-baryon, which has been missing from the LHCb baryon spectrum since 2012, has now been fully explored through a detailed study. By analyzing the decay of $D^+ \to K^- K^+ K^-$, researchers have constrained the mass and width of the $\Omega_b(4919)^-$ baryon. The resulting limits on its mass and width are  Standard models predict multiple states for the $\Omega_b(4919)^-$ baryon, and further analysis is required to determine which signal corresponds to which state.

Compartmental epidemiological models typically assume random person-to-person interactions and extensive mixing of the population, which can inaccurately represent the rapid transmission of infectious diseases in confined spaces like public transportation. A new probabilistic framework was developed for environments with moderate populations, such as buses, trains, and airports, that assumes high levels of interaction mixing. While this alternative framework seems beneficial, we show that its utility is questionable, as the difference between its outcomes and those from simulation-based methods with more realistic dynamics is substantial. Notably, even though this mixing framework yields a substantially expedited computation, its advantage is questionable given the comparable speed of modern computational systems. Furthermore, we found that the mixing framework's results can be efficiently transformed into near-optimal estimates following the breakdown of mixing assumptions, however, these estimates remain substantially less accurate than directly obtaining them through simulated scenarios. Lastly, we discovered that the framework's significant computational speed benefit arises from its ability to aggregate similar transmission patterns, whereas employing more efficient solving methods on the resulting system yields comparable substantial computational savings.

The concepts of quantum vacuum diffraction and birefringence have been proposed for more than two decades, predicting that the quantum vacuum can influence high-energy particle interactions and cause variations in the particle's spin and polarization. If these phenomena can be confirmed experimentally, they could potentially be detected by analyzing data from existing accelerator experiments, including those at the Large Hadron Collider and the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory. By examining relevant data sets, we found that current detection methods contain flaws which can also be found in previous proposals, and we propose an statistical framework for testing the validity of the quantum vacuum diffraction and birefringence phenomena. Additionally, this framework can be applied to other theoretical concepts, such as extra spatial dimensions, and we discuss the challenges and future possibilities in detecting these theories.

This note presents an innovative technique to swiftly determine the point coordinate
information for highly symmetric polyhedra in three-dimensional space, whose symmetry
properties are defined by the action of a transitive group on their faces. The method
can be utilized to swiftly obtain the Eisenlohr-Farris method's results for the
icosaeder, dodecaeder, and any other polyhedron that exhibits complete transitivity.

We've explored the concepts of semantically secure encryption (SSE) and indistinguishability-based secure encryption (IBE) in accordance with the Guidelines for Cryptographic Studies. We've discovered that under classical computation, these two notions are equivalent and differ quantitatively from one another by at most an extra bit of information. Under subexponential computation, they are distinct even qualitatively and we establish an advantage conversion rate of approximately 2^-k, where 'k' represents the number of bits in the message length. We also find that if certain strictly stronger notions of encryption, which we call secure encryption (IBE) and unclonable semantic security (USSE), are indistinguishable, then so are SSE and IBE, given specific circuit size constraints on adversaries. We prove that IBE is strictly weaker than IBE and we demonstrate that IBE falls short of USSE by approximately 2^-k in advantage conversion rate. We additionally discuss the relationship between these four notions and homomorphic encryption.

Physical layer security, an emerging authentication and secret sharing method, relies on unique physical characteristics of communication channels to generate a shared key between a transmitter and receiver. Although traditionally, the transmitted signals are crucial to forming the shared key, this approach faces several challenges, including high processing costs, vulnerable key extraction, and variable communication efficiency. To overcome these shortcomings, we propose a novel verification scheme that utilizes the inherent noise of the channel as its unique feature. Experimental results show that this method yields an efficient shared key while maintaining security, with minimal overhead and a comparable bit rate to traditional methods.

We propose a new system, twisted bilayer $T{{M}}{{D}}_2$, where the layers are rotated $168^\circ$ relative to each other, that exhibits flat-band SPJs. The flat-band in our model arises from the coupling of two interlayer dipole oscillations, which is a more robust mechanism than the stress-induced dipole coupling used in other systems. First principles calculations show that electrons in certain valleys can induce two types of bound states, 'in-phase' and 'anti-phase', corresponding to high and low work function states, respectively. The high energy state decays into the low energy state through the release of surface phonons, which is a signature of the SPJ phenomenon. The intensity of thisPhonon sideband can be increased up to $10^{-3}$ times the electron-hole recombination rate by adjusting the twist angle and chemical composition, enabling experimental verification of this mechanism.

This research paper confirms that gradient Ricci solitons on a Sasakian manifold that have the property of being almost conformal are equivalent to being harmonic. We also establish a link between harmonic and steady state gradient Ricci solitons under this condition. A specific example of such a soliton is provided, and a formula is derived for the potential function under the assumption that the soliton is both harmonic and shrinking. A necessary and sufficient condition for a harmonic harmonic gradient Ricci soliton to be shrinking is also obtained.

The nature of solar wind gusts and their impact on celestial bodies' ionospheres and magnetospheres remains relatively uncharted territory. This paper explores how these phenomena may vary across different celestial bodies with magnetospheres, from large planets like Jupiter to small ones like Mars. It examines key factors determining the response of a planet's magnetosphere to solar wind variations, including the presence of an intrinsic magnetic field, and how this influences the boundaries of the magnetosphere. Despite initial assumptions that the boundaries would react linearly to solar wind fluctuations, it's now clear that the complex structure of the magnetosphere leads to non-intuitive outcomes. For instance, planets with intrinsic magnetic fields, such as Earth, experience a more pronounced impact on their dayside magnetosphere during sudden solar wind changes, whereas planets without these fields, like Mars, may see their upstream magnetosphere expanded by hundreds of radii and have a less noticeable response. This paper aims to clarify the physics behind these phenomena and gather relevant historical data to facilitate future comparisons.

Spin-orbit proximity effect involves transfer of large spin-orbit coupling from one material to another with lower spin-orbit coupling when they form a interface. Recent research has focused on increasing the spin-orbit coupling in magnetic layers by creating a thin layer of high spin-orbit coupling material adjacent to the magnetic layer. This research aims to analyze the impact of spin-orbit coupling rate on the anomalous Hall effect in cobalt films topped with thin layers of bismuth. Experimental measurements were conducted to examine longitudinal and edge resistivity components of the anomalous Hall effect, which were theoretically modeled using the Landau-Lifshitz-Blotecka equations taking into consideration the materials' electron distribution, magnetic field-induced electron polarization, and spin-orbit coupling. Measurements and modeling revealed that the spin-orbit coupling transfer influences the anomalous Hall effect in cobalt/bismuth samples by altering the electron polarization in cobalt near the bismuth/ cobalt boundary, affecting the magnitude and direction of the anomalous Hall effect, and potentially controlled by changing the electron distribution in bi or cobalt Co layer and high mobility electron in disordered bi film which can be achieved by altering mobility in bi film or doping in cobalt.

This study presents analytical solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in complex, generalized potential fields, specifically the generalized Mie-like potential, in multiple dimensions. Utilizing Jumarie type fractional derivatives, researchers successfully obtained solutions and corresponding energy levels for a quantum system. The analysis demonstrates the applicability of the proposed method through graph visualizations and mathematical proofs of convergence.

We have developed a novel approach to improve neural network models by treating them as Lipschitz consistent functions and utilizing this as a form of regularization. This method is particularly useful for preventing overfitting in scenarios with limited data availability. We have formulated our approach by minimizing the maximum output variation caused by slight changes to the input data, a concept that is computationally challenging to handle directly. To overcome this, we have created an efficient algorithm to constrain neural networks by optimizing the Chebyshev distance between the network and a linear function. This approach is computationally tractable and can be solved using standard convex solvers. The results indicate that this approach significantly enhances the performance of neural networks in scenarios with limited data, while also preventing overconfident predictions and excessive model complexity.

Sequential neural network models are being used in the construction of part-of-speech taggers,
where the aim is to assign grammatical categories to words within a given text.
Neural network-based taggers rely on capturing syntactic relationships,
agreements between words, and semantic connections to accurately classify words.
Sequential neural network models, such as Long Short-Term Memory networks,
have been criticized for struggling with distant dependency relations.
To assess the capabilities of these models in capturing agreement,
we tested them on a Charsvane-based corpus, which provided a valuable resource.
Our experiments revealed that RNNs can perform well on local agreement but
experience more difficulty with non-local agreement, particularly when verb
tags are determined by the subject and the object.
However, we found that incorporating distant information through back connections
or utilizing character-level embedding can enhance the models' verb-tagging accuracy.

A globally distributed network of telescopes worked cooperatively to closely monitor the planet HD 8066 b's exceptionally bright transit. This observation involved multiple instruments which recorded the transit's start, middle, and end, providing a chance to refine the timing of future transits. This opportunity is crucial for perfectly calibrating the radial velocity and astrometric measurements that the Joint Almanac aims to use. Furthermore, this observation is crucial for planning effective observations of the planet using the James Webb Space Telescope. By analysing light curves from multiple telescopes, the team was able to derive precise timings for the transit, assuming a circular orbit and using only the transit data. These measurements led to the determination of the time since the beginning of the orbit (T0) and the orbital period (P) of the planet. These measurements were able to accurately predict the highly unusual 2019 T10.14 transit seen by the Hubble Space Telescope, as well as upcoming transits in 2022 and beyond. The team was able to accurately predict the transit by combining the previous measurements with their own. This accurate prediction is crucial for observing the planet HD 8066 b with the James Webb Space Telescope. By using all available data, the team was able to accurately predict the transit in 2022 and beyond. These predictions are crucial for effectively using the James Webb Space Telescope to observe the planet HD 8066 b.

The ability to analyze and manipulate game play through statistical models can serve as a foundation for creating engaging video games. -Based metrics, derived from these models, can determine game dynamics and influence player experience. -By leveraging the underlying structure of sports play, we can develop more realistic and adaptable training programs. -A specific application involves using a Bayesian probabilistic graph to model games, allowing for the prediction of play sequences and the assessment of individual player contributions. -In this context, we can fine-tune the rehabilitation process for injured athletes by adjusting the probability of occurring actions and incorporating real-game data to gradually readapt them to actual sporting environments.

This work estimates the phase-field approximation of functional classes on broken configurations, utilizing Gamma-convergence, to enable variational methods for high-dimensional problems. We extend previous results by Brokate and Stehlé to a broader context, obtaining an $\varepsilon$-approximation of a specific functional, originally defined on maps with singularities, by a modified version of it, evaluated on nearly identical maps. We then evaluate its implications, particularly in the context of modeling plastic deformation.

We've studied the Drell-Yan process for producing heavy quarks, specifically top-antitop pairs, from proton collisions at various energy levels. We've considered a scenario where a third-generation vector leptoquark exists. This leptoquark can decay into a top quark and the opposite charge of the relevant lepton. If these particles are created in pairs through quark scattering, they can also create heavy leptoquarks via the Drell-Yan process. We've analyzed the effects of adding extra gluons to a top quark's final state. This allows for more accurate predictions for experiments at the Large Hadron Collider.

Radiological imaging techniques are extensively utilized in the diagnosis of diseases and the monitoring of therapeutic interventions. However, their extensive use contributes to significant patient exposure to ionizing radiation. Our research focuses on reducing this risk in PET imaging by developing a PET synthesis model from CT and optical imaging images. Our approach employs a reduced-dose PET model trained with the assistance of a reduced-dose training dataset alongside a high-dose reference dataset, in order to mitigate the negative effects of data distribution discrepancies. Our approach incorporates probability distributions into the generator and the adversarial network to model data distribution uncertainties, allowing the model to learn from both reduced-dose and high-dose data. Additionally, our approach includes an explicit regulation term that minimizes the mean squared error between the predictions of the reduced-dose and high-dose networks. Experimental results indicate that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of performance and accuracy.

This research focuses on rational, customizable agents who can modulate the level of personal information disclosure. We examine the equilibrium effects of rational customization, considering both fully and partially observable states, and develop a novel, scalable method to train and evaluate these agents.

A key finding reveals that rational agents, through limited privacy control, can significantly reduce their information transmission rate to the environment, resulting in substantial customization benefits and enhanced privacy. Furthermore, our study explores the potential of partial privacy controls in achieving nearly optimal balances between customization and privacy.

We validate our approach using diverse environments, including GridWorld, MuJoCo continuous walking, and Amazon Web Services, and observe that our framework produces uniquely scalable agents. When presented with a new environment, these agents perform better than agents without customization capabilities.

We also contrast our work with self-modifying agents in related literature, highlighting the practical applications of partial privacy controls in limiting data disclosure to environments.

In summary, our study demonstrates the valuable effects of limited privacy controls on fully customizable rational agents, bringing us closer to creating customizable AI systems in a privacy-conscious manner.

A well-established psycholinguistic theory called Centering Theory (CT) can be adapted to create scoring systems for coreference resolution, but its effectiveness in current neural coreference resolution models remains unclear. By utilizing multi-task learning and advanced preprocessing techniques, we investigated whether CT-preprocessed inputs could be effectively handled by standard coreference resolution neural networks. Our findings indicate that creating CT-preprocessing frameworks is feasible and that incorporating CT features into loss functions after creating CT scores for all sentence element pairs during training can lead to better performance on low-resource languages or sentences with limited discourse markers, particularly when using a unified framework. Furthermore, adding a pre-processing step that calculates CT scores and integrating specific aspects of the CT framework into the training process can enhance the models' coreference resolution capabilities, prompting further research into the role of CT and other cognitive science theories in coreference resolution within a neural context.

This lecture will introduce the concept of upward planarity in directed graphs,
upward planar embeddings preserve left (right) order of edges around each vertex,
and we will focus on finding minimum subset of edges to make a graph upward planar.
This problem is known to be NP-hard and we will examine its parameterized approach,
particularly in relation to two parameters: the minimum subset size and another parameter k.
When limited to binary graphs, we will discuss how the problem is FPT parameterized by its second parameter k,
and introduce the recent development of exponential fixed-parameter algorithm for general graphs,
which produces a solution with a runtime involving the first parameter b^m where b is a constant yet undefined,

In computer science research, configuring experimental environments is a labor-intensive process that is crucial for both newly hired researchers and established team members. To reduce this burden, we have developed an automated tool called GoodSystem, which is open-source and runs on Jupyter notebooks. This program not only streamlines the process of replicating results but also makes it easier for new members to join a project by automatically handling the setup of required system components. We incorporated GoodSystem into our own workflow and are eager for feedback from the community to further enhance the tool's functionality.

In the large-N limit of U(N) SYM, the group N^2 exhibits a significant entanglement with an operator basis that includes all possible combinations of gluons, rendering the large-N syzygy ineffective for diagonalizing the Hamiltonian. The entanglement between the operator basis and the energy eigenstates becomes even more pronounced for the adjoint representation, where the degree of mixing increases. The benefit of expanding the basis to include all possible combinations of gluons in the fundamental representation, as seen in the 't Hooft expansion, becomes irrelevant due to the extensive entanglement. The large-N entanglement also exhibits a deep syzygy, where the more the operator basis is extended, the more the system resembles N (not large-N), behaving similarly to the theory with retarded interactions. The increase in entanglement during N -> infinity results in the syzygy converting from infinity to a finite value. The large-N entanglement has significant implications for understanding the local syzygy in black hole evaporation and the retarded interactions inside the black hole.

Recently, more businesses are investing in IoT projects that allow them to monitor and optimize their facilities internally. The main challenge in these projects is creating the coordination framework to manage and connect a large number of IoT sensors and devices. Traditionally, sensors provide data for a specific location, while devices like WiFi access points can indicate proximity to multiple devices, but handling this massive amount of data has proven difficult. The aim of this paper is to present a novel method to utilize machine learning to process and clean raw data from WiFi signals to identify their physical distance, thereby creating a more efficient data source for clustering techniques to optimize network setup in similar environments. Our approach is presented through numerical results obtained from real-world data collected in a typical office setting.

We employ simplified models to investigate the stability of a spherical structure, often referred to as a Dyson Shell, located around a black hole in a flat spacetime environment. Specifically, we focus on shells that enclose non-charged, pressureless matter under the influence of gravity. Our analysis reveals that the accumulation of a sufficient amount of charge within the interior of the shell can maintain its structural integrity. However, in cases where the interior contains a Schwarzschild black hole, the application of sufficient internal pressure can achieve a similar effect, allowing the shell to remain stable.

In contract management, detecting when service levels agreed upon in SLAs are not met is crucial. Traditional methods of detection often rely on a centralized approach, which has drawbacks, including the risk of a single point of failure and the limitation of requiring a trusted authority. To address the dependence on a centralized system, this paper proposes a novel, innovative approach utilizing peer-to-peer (P2P) technology to identify SLA breaches. This approach also ensures that no single entity has access to the entire dataset, which is achieved through the integration of secure P2P technology and homomorphic encryption. A conceptual design for this approach is illustrated with the aid of a logical schema and a Case Study on ERP-as-a-Service, while the feasibility and effectiveness of utilizing P2P technology for detection purposes are examined through the lenses of capability, reliability, and efficiency.

The disruptive beam layout phenomenon, which has been identified in standard linear accelerators, has also emerged in energy recovery linear accelerators (ERLs).  Building upon a vector potential model that explains beam disruption instability (BDI) in linear accelerators, this study has analyzed the stable operational regions of ERLs using a multi-mode approach and validated it with particle simulations.  As a result, our study reveals that, unlike traditional linear accelerators where only specific beam configurations exhibit stability, ERLs exhibit stable operational regions for a broader range of configurations.  The existence of these stable operational regions is attributed to the presence of beam beam coupling modes resulting from multiple passes between linac and cavity in ERLs.  Furthermore, under certain conditions, higher order modes could be reutilized to stabilize beam disruption instability (BDI) in linear accelerators by adjusting the linear beam beam coupling coefficient.  The implications of these findings may allow for optimized design and performance of particle physics experiments utilizing energy recovery linear accelerators.

Proposed scintillator detectors featuring thin, enriched in hydrogen CH targets and wavelength-shifting fibers could potentially overcome the low detection efficiency hurdles that currently impede the neutron cross-section data availability needed to refine the astrophysical JINA REACT database. A prototype detector using CB and CZ scintillators has shown that CZ crystals exhibit nearly ten times the light output of CB crystals when exposed to minimum bias protons, although their neutron-to proton signal ratio remains roughly the same. The detector's 3D detection capability has proven effective at distinguishing neutrons from the photon background induced by scattered protons and excited CH atoms through directional light signals, while also reducing the required data acquisition time to seconds - a significant improvement over conventional detectors requiring minutes to hours. Furthermore, the high resolution and rapid data processing capability of these detectors have proven useful in suppressing the photon background, thus improving the purity of the reaction data and proving their potential applicability to future experiments on the China Jinping Underground Laboratory.

To understand the start of planetary formation, we need to know how quickly dust particles come together. In this research, we examined how dry and water-containing ice particles react when they collide, considering dry silicates and mix of silicates plus water ice. The experiments were performed at various temperatures mimicking those found in protoplanetary discs. It was found that for dry particles, sticking occurs at lower temperatures but adding water ice increases the force of sticking at moderate temperatures. However, at higher temperatures the force of sticking decreases due to thermal motion of the particles. The results indicate a key factor in the early stages of planet formation, particularly in cold regions of protoplanetary discs where water ice is present, and has implications for material processing and thermal movement of particles as they move through different parts of a protoplanetary disc.

One must be cautious when relying on dimension reduction methods like Fisher's Discriminant Analysis (FDA), especially in contexts such as image classification, which typically involves a large number of features and a relatively small number of classes. This issue arises because FDA's primary assumption often does not hold under these conditions. Specifically, the assumption of a linear relationship between classes can be complex to visualize and understand, particularly when dealing with a large number of features. This R package is designed to assist in analyzing the Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA), which was proposed to address limitations of FDA in research and teaching settings. It enables users to visualize and evaluate the effectiveness of FDA and LFDA by generating heat maps, scatter plots, and other graphical representations, which can be used to identify where the models may fail and guide further research or teaching discussions.

Multi-robot coordination through motion planning and evasion is typically complicated by environmental constraints and dynamic barriers. To tackle these challenges in a broader context, this research introduces an innovative framework that encompasses nonlinear constraints and obstacles in static or moving forms. This framework focuses on learning and adapting the relationship between a tracker and an evadee using data from multiple robots, enabling the evader to mimic the tracker while evading capture. A key aspect of this framework involves exploiting the inherent stability of Kalman filters to ensure safe capture within a predetermined bound. Theoretical and practical validations of this framework are provided, including at least three validation cases that demonstrate its effectiveness and reliability.

We have calculated the one-loop central-emission vertex for two colorless bosons, which can be applied to various amplitudes within N=4 super Yang-Mills (QCD). This calculation applies to any spin point in N=4 super Yang-Mills (QCD), and we have specifically determined the one-loop central-emission vertex for two scalars at the point of interest for N=4 super Yang-Mills (QCD), which can be related to various gravitational interactions. Additionally, we have derived the corresponding one-loop central-emission vertex for two gluons based on a method that relates gravitational interactions to N=4 super Yang-Mills (QCD) interactions.

Within the topological Rashba Hubbard model on a 2D square lattice, we've identified a novel phase of spin-singlet superfluidity that exhibits Majorana zero-modes at the corners of the Brillouin zone. This occurs in contrast to the well-known spin-triplet topological superfluid phase, which requires spin symmetry breaking and is not permitted in certain systems like cold atoms on a Rashba lattice. Utilizing a time-reversal-invariant extension of the Fulde-Fermer-Letterto-Kosteckal scenario, we demonstrated that the spin-singlet topological superfluidity is attainable for both filling levels of one electron per site. Additionally, we showed that Rashba spin-orbit coupling plays a crucial role in expanding the spin-singlet topological superfluid phase, which could be detected through spin-singlet pair-density waves and a non-vanishing winding number in the spin-resolved Berker networks.

By combining terahertz spectroscopy and x-ray scattering, we recovered lost data from a long-standing experiment and performed in-depth comparisons with various high-temperature cuprate superconductors. We examined how the intra-unit cell flux vortex states behave as they evolve from square to square roots of $T_\textrm{c}$ patterns, using x-ray scattering. Infrared and terahertz measurements yielded conflicting c-axis resistivity results, with distinct variations in the normal and superconducting states. These findings indicate that the unit cell's intra-flux vortex states exhibit remarkable superconducting coherence near $T_\textrm{c}$, demonstrating potential for evidence of the normal superconducting gap, pseudogap, and Hahn gaps.

The behavior of molten polymer brushes on stretched substrates can be modeled as a collection of stretched, molten chains. When an indentation or protrusion of the substrate extends beyond a certain length, it becomes impossible to form molten polymer bridges in the surrounding area. It is conjectured that these excluded regions, where molten polymers cannot exist, have a maximum extent. However, proving this maximum exists in cases where the stretched substrate has a complex shape remains elusive. In this research, we provide a method to demonstrate the existence of this maximum directly through numerical simulations, using a finite-difference approach to solve the Euler-Lagrange equations. This allows us to analytically examine the stability of the polymer brush in statically stretched, molten surfaces.

A graph G is considered resolvable by a set of vertices S if every other node in the graph can be uniquely identified by its relative distance to the vertices in S. This concept was initially explored by Chartrand et al. and later expanded upon by Slater and Harary. In 2022, we define a shortened metric dimension, denoted as $\rho(G)$, for a graph G. This new dimension represents the minimum number of vertices required to resolve the graph using only non-infinite distances. We establish an upper bound for $\rho(G)$ as 2 for certain graphs and an upper bound of 4 for general graphs. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between $\rho(G)$ and traditional metric dimension and discover that they share the same property when certain conditions are met. This work also demonstrates that graphs with a shortened metric dimension of 1 are precisely those with a traditional metric dimension of 1.

Utilizing machine learning techniques to analyze all-sky images captured by the Fermi-LAT gamma-ray telescope, this research develops two crucial tools: an enhanced background map and improved detection of transient sources. By examining a six-year dataset from 2008 to 2014, the researchers employ classification algorithms to identify variable sources, specifically those exhibiting significant changes in brightness. Utilizing an independent test set, it is demonstrated that a decision tree classifier can produce a highly accurate background chart, significantly outperforming a naive approach and reducing misclassifications of dark regions. Furthermore, the researchers discuss the application of dimensionality reduction techniques to extract time series data from moving source light curves. Ultimately, this work paves the way for advanced image recognition and source tracking using data from the gamma-ray telescope.

A new voting rule called Enhanced Serial Dictatorship has already been subtly described in prior research, which we have now examined and promoted. This rule has now been clarified and its properties fully explored, including the number of necessary alternatives in relation to the number of alternatives required by Anonymous Enhanced Serial Dictatorship and the Half-Fullness Theorem. Additionally, we have conducted a small-scale quantitative examination of Half-Fullness within Random Respondent Order (RRO).

We developed an algorithm to identify binaries in time-exposures from the Pan-STARRS1 and its 30-meter companion telescope, focusing on objects within the 0.4 to 9.4 arcmin/orbit diameter range. The algorithm automatically detects contact binaries and those with offsets up to 10 arcseconds, identifying 41 candidates including 24 clearly visible binaries. The list of candidates is publicly available at the given URL, and we highlighted the objects with the most varied orbits. Notable examples include the first 4-Pan small-time binary, the 2012 SA2, which exhibits the shortest 4-Pan detection period object, the 2004 BL2, which has the most extensive orbit, and the 2015 DO14, which has the highest estimated absolute magnitude. Furthermore, our analysis revealed discrepancies between the observed and predicted size distributions, particularly in the 11-100 m interval, and found the binary frequency of near-Earth asteroids to be higher than that of Main Belt asteroids.

Using a unified framework, we assess the validity of a specific modeling approach for analyzing continuous outcomes in complex social networks. This framework considers various forms of unmeasured factors that may influence the outcome and are not accounted for in the model, such as properties intrinsic to the nodes. To test this approach, we employ a Bayesian method called stacked sampling, which takes into consideration the interconnections between the variables that influence each other. This allows us to evaluate the test's accuracy in scenarios similar to those observed in real networks, particularly in the area of measuring peer effects. In this application, our research examines the conclusion reached by an article published in a reputable journal, which claimed that the evidence for peer effects was lacking when examining the choice of university by high school graduates. Our analysis challenges this conclusion.

This study introduces novel expressions for the Variable-Order Riemann-Liouville integral, specifically I^α_t(a), applied to constant and linear functions. In addition to this, we derive novel results for the Variable-Order Riemann-Liouville derivative, specifically D^α_t(a), applied to constant and linear functions. Furthermore, we derive an identity for the Variable-Order Riemann-Liouville integral, specifically I^α_t(a), applied to the Variable-Order Riemann-Liouville derivative, specifically D^β_t(a), applied to a differentiable function f. In addition to this, we derive an identity for the Variable-Order Riemann-Liouville integral, specifically I^α_t(a), applied to the Variable-Order Riemann-Liouville derivative, specifically D^β_t(a), applied to a differentiable function f. In addition to this, we derive an identity for the Variable-Order Riemann-Liouville derivative, specifically D^α_t(a), applied to a Variable-Order Riemann-Liouville integral, specifically I^β_t(a), applied to a differentiable function f. The concept of spatial signal identification has gained significant interest in various applications, including environmental monitoring and seismic research. This area is expanding, and particularly promising is the development of spatially variant filtering techniques. This technology could allow for more precise estimation of time-varying signals from sensor arrays arranged in grids or other configurations, by accounting for the unique behavior of individual sensors. Unfortunately, existing research on spatial signal identification hasn't produced a comprehensive understanding of how the sensor arrangement and the method of data collection affect performance. This work addresses that gap by providing a thorough examination of the stability and convergence rates of a grid-based system that allows for time-dependent convergence. It also explores the potential of this type of filtering in real-world applications, and compares its effectiveness to alternative methods of data collection and sensor arrangements.

Einstein X-ray telescopes, such as XRTE on the Chandra mission and RXIT on the RXTE mission, excel at collecting high-quality X-ray spectra and high-resolution spatial images of celestial objects. To analyze these multi-dimensional datasets effectively, researchers need user-friendly software that can visualize data in 2D and 3D, create light curves, and generate spectral plots. Our newly updated version of RCSEDv2, an open-source online toolset, provides such functionality via web browsers, allowing users to customize their visualizations and export high-quality graphics. Developed using HTML5, JavaScript, and Apache D3, RCSEDv2 is built upon the visualization framework established in RCSED, and we have now expanded its capabilities to include features from the Chandra Interactive Graphics System (CIGS) and the RXTE Interactive Graphics System (RIXS).

The Southern Atlantic Ocean's formation is attributed to a Central Atlantic Magmatic Province, after which the North and South American plates separated, initiating the Atlantic Mid-Ocean Ridge's activity in the South Atlantic. This work analyzes computer models and plate tectonic data to clarify the rate and direction of plate movement along the Southern Atlantic Mid-Ocean Ridge, from its beginning to the Reykjanes Peninsula-Azores Triple Junction in 1960. During periods of high ridge expansion, plates moved apart quickly, creating normal faulting and long, parallel fissures. In periods of low ridge expansion, the plate movement slowed down, creating shear fractures and limited self-sustaining expansions. The existence of large, collapsed sections of the floor in certain segments of the South Atlantic Mid-Ocean Ridge can be explained by the size and direction of the self-sustaining expansions relative to the surrounding regions of low expansion. The rate and pattern of plate movement along the Southern Atlantic Mid-Ocean Ridge are irregular and complex, varying widely in different parts of the ridge and changing frequently with time.

When using segmentation algorithms, distinguishing the boundary region of the target is a major challenge. This difficulty is compounded in self-supervised learning scenarios, where the modeling technique is required to accurately capture the boundary region without labeled data for precise evaluation. As an advanced self-supervised learning methodology, section-cutting information maximization has been proven particularly effective in generating high-quality segmentations. This technique's ability to model the distribution of anatomical structures makes it comparable to the global information flow in U-Net, yet its advantage over USSM lies in incorporating boundary-sensitive information. To further enhance section-cutting information maximization, we introduce additional loss functions based on neighboring superpixels and sliding windows, which enable the model to learn detailed boundary regions. Our proposed method demonstrates superior performance on several datasets, outperforming both supervised and self-supervised learning baselines for segmenting multiple organs in CT images and abdominal MR images.

To effectively cooperate with a modern Dungeons and Dragons group, our main character learns through reinforcement learning how to use their abilities and guide the game's progress with purpose and consideration for others, ultimately demonstrating theoretically that using Intents and Theory-of-Mind can be beneficial in both the long and short term.

This paper提出在词向量空间的变化中发现新语义 shift 的无监督学习方法。我们的方法能够识别出字典中的语义群体中发生显著变化的一部分词汇，这些词汇可能代表新的概念。为了展现有效性，我们进行了广泛的实验，包括使用新闻语料库对维基百科语义群体进行测试、使用不同的语料库对 AG-NEWS 语义群体进行测试、利用历史语料库训练 BAbI 语义群体以及评估方法在 BAbI 语义群体上的表现。结果证明，我们的方法能够精确地发现词汇语义变化。

We propose a new set of functions related to the momentum transverse part that you can derive from the parton distribution functions to partons maintaining symmetry. These functions can be related to the functions that describe correlations between the motion of a particle and the momentum transverse part. A set of functions that describe correlations between the motion of a particle and the momentum transverse part of a nucleon is also derived from the functions that describe the motion of two gluons transverse to the momentum within the nucleon, is also discussed.

The three-dimensional structure and knot type of a knotted protein can be
transformed into an equivalent, simplified topological model. Identifying the
folding pathways of knotted proteins has significant implications for
understanding how these complex structures form. Recent simulations and
experimental evidence reveal bending pathways as the primary folding
mechanism of knotted proteins. These pathways can be distinguished from other
structures due to their minimal energy and uniqueness. In this research, we
examine bending structures of knotted proteins from previous studies, identifying
their essential features through topological analysis. Notably, we discover that
only bending structures maintain the knot type during deformation, setting them
apart from other configurations. This discovery leads to a unique selection of
pathways for folding into specific shapes.

To address the mystery of why the universe's expansion started 4.6 billion years after the Big Bang, researchers propose introducing an early dark energy component. By combining data from the Planck satellite and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey, we can constrain the parameters of this component. Using a general parameterization and analyzing the planar data and the BOSS data, researchers found significant limitations on the density of early dark energy. Specifically, their research indicates that the early dark energy cannot exceed a certain percentage of the current critical density of the universe. This research provides a valuable contribution to the study of early dark energy, which is ranked among the most mysterious components of the universe.

We've established that the symplectic mapping class groups of low-dimensional torus bundles have a large finitely generated subgroup that's isomorphic to a Heisenberg group, which isn't a finite index subgroup. In contrast, we've also shown that the symplectic mapping class groups of certain blown-up tori in dimensions up to 6 contain subgroups that are isomorphic to the integer Heisenberg groups $H_k(\mathbb Z)$ for any $k \geq 2$, which have infinite rank.

A rigorous mathematical proof of the Nambu-Goldstone theorem in both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories is achieved using mass-spectrum analysis and an analitycity property, with sufficient assumptions on the underlying spacetime. The analitycity property can be substituted with the Bethe ansatra equation in specific model systems, which already have established proofs. However, the proof of the theorem reveals the exclusion of massless Nambu-Goldstone particles in systems with restored symmetries through either sufficient conditions on the mass-spectrum or the Bethe ansatra equation, as these conditions inherently imply the existence of an energy gap below the symmetry restoration point, thus providing the proof of the theorem as an unintended outcome of the analysis of the mass-spectrum.

NLP models make decisions based on intricate patterns, but these patterns can be difficult for humans to comprehend. To facilitate clearer understanding, researchers are exploring the concept of counting hypothetical alternatives, also referred to as "p-CRA". This concept, however, is laborious to evaluate and requires significant time and resources. To make this evaluation more straightforward, researchers are examining the capability of NLP models to spontaneously generate hypothetical alternatives, specifically combinations of words that produce the same outcome but differ in composition. This capability is referred to as "phrasal discoidility" (P-DISCO). In a surprising finding, researchers discovered that most NLP models struggled to successfully generate these hypothetical alternatives. To further investigate this capability, researchers designed a novel evaluation method, "phrasal discoidility" (P-DISCO), and discovered that models could only marginally exceed random chance levels in generating these alternatives. To address this limitation, researchers developed a novel approach, "Discoidility-Aware Generation" (DAG), that significantly enhanced the models' ability to generate these hypothetical alternatives. In a remarkable result, DAG achieved up to a 25% increase in successful generation of these alternatives, showcasing the potential of NLP models to spontaneously generate hypothetical alternatives that are linked to their current outcomes.

The total coloring of a graph G involves assigning colors to both its vertices and edges under the condition that colors for adjacent elements must differ. The concept of a distinguishing total coloring was first introduced by Karo\'s and recently extensively studied due to its relevance in anti-spam filtering. This study aims to determine the sum-distinguishing total choosivity (SDTC) for various types of circulant graphs by determining the distinguishing total chromatic index (DTCHI) and the distinguishing total chromatic number (SDTCG) for them. To achieve this, properties of circulant graphs and their adjacency matrices are utilized. Specifically, adjacent sum-distinguishing edge-colored (ASDEG) and neighborhood sum-distinguishing vertex colored (NSVGG) are defined. To demonstrate the feasibility of 6-ASDEn for even integers n greater than or equal to 10, and 5-NSVGG, we provide appropriate coloring schemes. Additionally, the inequalities 6≤ASDEI≤7, and 5≤NSVGI≤6, and the equality NSVGI=5 for odd values of n, are proven. Based on these findings, the bounding inequalities for the SDTCG of circulant graphs are determined as 6≤ASDCGn ≤7, and for odd values of n, the SDTCG is equal to the NSVGG, which is also equal to 5.

In this research, we studied how different types of epithelial growth - remote, van der Waals, and pinhole - are balanced in heterostructures combining rotor Heusler films with either raw or oxide-terminated sapphire substrates. We found that pinhole growth occurs when the energy of the Heusler film and the oxide layer on the sapphire are both high, but growth is possible even without the help of an oxide buffer at a specific ROR Heusler composition. Furthermore, the presence of a Al_2O_3 buffer alters the lattice strain in the Heusler film, allowing it to match the underlying sapphire lattice more closely. We discovered that an optimal heating range of 600-700 C, along with a precise control of the vapor pressure of the ROR Heusler source, results in quality Heusler film growth. Notably, this optimal range differs from the temperatures at which the Heusler source itself is stable.

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it contains all codewords formed by linear combinations (using coefficients from $\Z_{p^2}$) of the code's generator matrix rows, where elements from $\Z_p$ are considered equivalent to their $\Z_{p^2}$ counterparts in this study. This paper delves into the macWilliams identity for $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes, along with studies of the null space and dimension of such a code. The article also examines how the dimension and ground set rank of a code are related, and introduces key definitions including that of irreducible blocks, subcodes, and code covers.

The dynamics of polymer plugs, utilized in enhanced oil recovery, have been extensively studied in laboratory settings. A key limitation in these studies arises from the unknown injection profile of the polymer, which significantly impacts the polymer's behavior. This research introduces a novel, continuous method for controlling the polymer injection rate, achieved by inserting the polymer cylinder axially into an oil cylinder using internal friction. The friction between the polymer and oil cylinders determines the speed at which the polymer advances, leading to a rate that remains consistently constant for a given internal friction coefficient, provided the polymer cylinder is completely enclosed within the oil cylinder. This method offers a simplified yet effective means of studying the polymer injection profile, which can be integrated into laboratory experiments for enhanced oil recovery applications.

A significant portion of datasets is tagged with a single label per instance, however, many such items actually match multiple labels. These multi-label cases are frequently overlooked during supervised training as they are categorized under a single positive category. Research into using datasets to train multi-label models from single-label tagged items is still in its early stages. In this paper, we initially examine the degree of multi-labelness present in two prominent object detection datasets, COCO and KITTI, then propose a novel algorithm to identify the overlooked multi-label items within these datasets. Our method ultimately identifies 11.4% of COCO and 18.3% of KITTI items as containing multiple labels despite being labeled with just one. We then collected additional labels for these items through a web interface. A model trained on the resulting data achieves a 0.425 Hall coefficient when evaluated against ensemble baselines.

This research investigates the time-fractional Cahn-Landau-Ginzburg equation,  
which arises in modeling various phenomena including the non-monotonic energy  
dissipation observed in viscoelastic materials. A upper bound for the rate of  
energy dissipation is shown to be asymptotically accurate as the time parameter  
approaches infinity. The proof of this result is shewn for both strong and weak  
solutions to the equation. Furthermore, a modified equation is derived from  
the original TFFPHE, which shares the same right-hand side and possesses an  
exact solution. A comparison is made between the exact and numerical solutions  
to this modified equation using the implicit tau method.

The generalized measurement process has been mathematically described through a specific type of algebraic structure consisting of four components: a C*-algebra, a positivity-preserving map, a subset of a positive definite functional, and a subset of a self-adjoint element. This specific structure forms a category denoted as CMT Hilb*. A functor connects the CMT Hilb* category to the algebraic operations of a C*-algebra, mapping it to its own category and retaining its natural transformations and monadic properties. Notable outcomes of this research are the discovery of a comonadic lifting and a Bialgebraic framework for states in a C*-algebra. The algebraic framework of Quantum Automata has been advanced by this theoretical discovery.

We predict long gamma-rays in high energy ranges from several nearby galaxies, specifically the S2 and S2-n2, which are the closest to Earth and possess strong magnetic fields surrounding their disks. These predictions apply to a broad range of galaxies that are the source of radio emissions, which are generated by the interaction of plasma in the disk with magnetic fields. Gamma-rays in high energy ranges are produced when particles are accelerated to extreme speeds, interacting with the surrounding environment and producing emission that can be detected by satellites like the Fermi-LAT. Our theory aligns with observed data from several galaxies, but we need more sensitive detection tools to confirm this in more cases and understand the underlying processes better.

This research reevaluates commonly used performance evaluation methods, such as Sharpe ratio and information ratio, by focusing on how portfolios are allocated across securities and linking these metrics to portfolio return behavior. It leverages the mean-reverting characteristics of asset returns, which the study finds aligns with the liquidity premium, to derive the portfolio return dynamics. The allocation framework can be expressed using the Lagrangian multiplier for the efficient frontier, and Monte Carlo simulations are employed to create realistic implementations. These simulations reveal that portfolio returns often follow exponential distributions, where the real-world performance metrics closely match the theoretical expectations established by the study. The research also discusses the limitations of popular portfolio evaluation measures and proposes the development of new indicators suited to portfolio optimization problems.

Making a diagnosis of heart conditions can be done by analyzing audio signals from listening to a patient's chest, but doing so accurately is complicated due to background noise and the varying way sound patterns appear in a waveform. A deep learning approach called HeartNet has been designed to identify normal heart sounds, despite the presence of noise, by using multiple networks that focus on different aspects of the data and learn from each other through a technique called knowledge distillation. Each heart condition is represented by a unique neural network that analyzes frequency information and temporal changes in a latent space, using autoencoders to manage data representation. A single teacher network learns to classify heart sounds from time-series data using a modified long short-term memory network, then shares its knowledge with the student networks through weighted loss functions during training. As a result, the teacher network and the multiple students are capable of accurately diagnosing heart conditions, even in noisy environments, from the data collected from a new open-access database called MIMOCHeart. Experimental results show that this approach outperforms existing methods in its tests.

The concept of using wearable devices to monitor health and prevent diseases is still in its infancy, and implementing these technologies using multiple devices poses a problem of sharing sensitive data for model improvement. A federated learning approach could potentially resolve this issue, but research into this method for wearable medical care is nearly nonexistent. In this paper, we propose FedHealth, a novel framework that incorporates federated transfer learning to enhance the performance of wearable medical monitoring systems. FedHealth allows for the sharing of raw data for initial training and allows participating devices to contribute to updating the model in a secure, encryption-based manner. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we conducted experiments using multiple wearable medical monitoring devices and found that FedHealth outperforms conventional methods in accuracy, with improvements of up to 5% compared to the previous record using federated learning. Furthermore, FedHealth achieves accuracy comparable to direct data sharing while avoiding the risks of leaking sensitive patient information.

Elevated moment portfolio optimization approaches, including risk measurement methods such as Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall, share similar mathematical principles. This paper explores a broader class of optimization problems based on higher-order moments, specifically examining the implications for risk measurement. By proposing an alternative method that considers only higher-order moments, we aim to refine the parameters of existing models and provide a framework for comparing the performance of different optimization techniques within this broader class. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, offering insights into the relationship between these methods from both a theoretical and practical perspective. This research paper seeks to bridge the gap between portfolio optimization techniques that focus on elevated moments and the domain of risk measurement.

We introduce the coincidence dilemma, a newly identified challenge in perspective taking that hasn't been discussed widely due to its connection to the well-documented perspective dilemma. Research has revealed that individuals have a limited ability to mentally simulate scenarios that contradict their current knowledge. We simulate the conditions required for accurately perceiving low-entropy worlds that are far from our own, by altering the natural tendency to consider high-entropy scenarios. Our experiments show that simulating a perspective dissimilar to our own is constrained by our models of possible worlds, and has significant implications for understanding the limitations of Bayesian perspective taking and the perspective dilemma.

This document outlines our system that streamlines the conversion of PDF files
into machine-readable formats, specifically for extracting data from scientific
publications. Our innovative solution utilizes AI to interpret and translate
complex layouts and writing styles, enabling a more efficient process compared
 to manual methods. We have also evaluated various input options and generated
 PDF invoices, demonstrating the versatility and versatility of our system.

We tackle the minimum cost problem under a toggleable control, where the cost follows a semi-martingale process that reacts sharply to abrupt control changes. Our work extends previous studies by addressing the specific challenge posed by C\^adl\^ag costs, which can lead to infeasible optimizations due to the potential for the cost process to toggle between values. To resolve this issue, we investigate the impact of toggle costs on optimal control and prove the existence of an optimal control that minimizes the expected cost at a given time. Under particular conditions, we demonstrate that the optimal control follows a smooth switching surface and derive the sensitivity of the cost with respect to time and initial conditions. Our results hold under more general assumptions, specifically those involving the expectation of the cost process.

In the leptoquark sector of the Standard Model's extension, current constraints from the lepton flavor changing decays and b-quark physics suggest that even leptoquark pair production could occur with sufficient intensity to be detected at the Large Hadron Collider. A comprehensive analysis has been conducted on the potential impacts of the presence of even leptoquark masses as low as 800 GeV, taking into consideration both their influence on flavor-changing decays and the potential for their production. Furthermore, an exploration has been undertaken on the potential for generating a dominant charged lepton flux from even leptoquark decay chains.

Sequential information such as scientific terminology helps enhance general knowledge and vocabulary in students. However, traditional methods for testing comprehension, like multiple-choice questions, do not effectively measure a learner's ability to apply their knowledge in a sequence. To address this limitation, we've developed an innovative approach to assess students' understanding of complex temporal sequences by using supervised learning techniques to generate multiple-choice questions. Using the Flenus system, we can generate multiple-choice questions from structured data sets containing temporal sequences. In this system, we've refined the use of carefully selected options to minimize the accuracy of random guesses while maximizing the accuracy of correct answers when paired with the correct answer key. As a result, our supervised learning approach improved performance on the scale by approximately 20% compared to baseline models.

We have developed a simple, non-radiative model to explain the low-excitation fine structure lines of carbon and nitrogen ions in some molecular gas reservoirs. Our analysis indicates that these lines are poorly explained by the standard photoionization model because their emissions cannot be adequately sustained even with increased rates of Lyman continuum photons. Instead, our findings reveal that these lines are substantially stimulated by the movement and heating of gas caused by the movement of the reservoirs' collapsing bulk. This kind of subthermal stimulation is commonly found (in approximately 50% of cases) in reservoirs with significant mass movements, particularly those exceeding $10^8$ solar masses and showing large velocities ($\sim 100$ km/s). The intensity of this stimulation is directly correlated with the amount of subthermal energy moving and heating the reservoirs, allowing them to accelerate and accelerate. The Subthermal model's predictions regarding the CO lines cannot be distinguished from those of the standard photoionization model, whereas the C{\sc i} lines and the N{\sc i} lines exhibit distinct, observable discrepancies. These discrepancies allow the Subthermal model to be tested and evaluated by the presence or absence of these lines in a variety of molecular gas reservoirs, such as the Taurus A reservoir. Furthermore, our analysis allows us to explain previous contradictory observational and theoretical findings.

Recent experimental data suggests that both the $K$ and $B$ anomalies can be addressed by introducing right-handed universal interactive quarks at the energy scale of 3-5 TeV.  If these quarks are the lowest energy representatives of their composite partners, then the strong interactions demand pairs of such quarks.  By selectively disabling the effective operators mediated by these quark doublets, we can derive the necessary lower energy quark triplet states.  The effectiveness of these triplet states in clarifying the $K$ and $B$ anomalies varies across different energy scales, with the 3 TeV scale failing to address the anomaly and the 5 TeV scale resolving both anomalies.

Given positive integers $k$ and $k'$, we determine the maximum number of pairs of real numbers that can be arranged such that the number of distinct distances between any two pairs has a limit of $k$, and for every distance, it can be repeated $k'$ times or less. This problem is related to a variant of the classic geometric series reconstruction problem from Erdos-Hajnal, which deals with arranging numbers based on their pairwise distances.

Musical instrument classification is essential in various applications including Music Production and Musical analysis. Although deep learning techniques have reached a high level of proficiency in this area, there's still room for enhancement, especially when dealing with a wide range of instruments. This research proposes a novel approach to improve performance in multi-instrument musical recognition by training the model on a limited number of specific instruments and then expanding it to identify additional instruments through cross-domain training. This technique demonstrates significant improvements in accuracy, achieving nearly 90% accuracy on 38 MIDI instruments, compared to an initial model's accuracy of 65%. The code for the model is openly accessible on a GitHub repository.

We call the challenge of providing accurate and complete answers to high-level, information-rich questions using only given source documents the Question Answering (QA) task. To perform well on such questions, models must grasp the nuanced background knowledge of their specific domain, including its specialized terminology and complex conceptual relationships. Unfortunately, publicly available datasets for information-rich questions are typically limited to a handful of topics due to the difficulty of collecting diverse, real-world data. To address this limitation, we have created a comprehensive dataset called ResearchQA, which contains more than 34,000 information-rich questions spanning 10 different fields and is made up of individual paragraphs from scholarly articles. This dataset is particularly useful for testing the ability of language models to handle difficult, research-level questions in diverse subject areas. As of now, it represents the largest publicly available dataset for such questions.

We have developed highly accurate approximations for the orbital period evolution of binaries in eccentric orbits within the post-Newtonian framework, specifically for low-order parameters in the quadrupole domain. These advancements enable a more precise study of populations of inspiralling binaries and their effect on pulsar timing arrays. However, they come with increased computational complexity, necessitating the use of adaptive algorithms to efficiently evaluate the four distinct PN parameters, which vary throughout an binary's eccentric orbit. As an illustration, we examine the impact of an equal mass, close elliptical binary on the PTA dataset and demonstrate that the greater precision it offers over alternative approximations, such as waveforms computed using Einstein Toolkit, can be easily reached with roughly one order of magnitude fewer CPU hours.

We establish that the asymptotic velocities of particles in the asymmetric simple exclusion process, located at the system's boundaries, conform to a Brownian motion while influenced by a simple exclusion process, scaled linearly with the system size's third power. This finding enables us to identify the speed distribution of particles under specific high-density conditions and provides a basis for developing the space-time q-TASEP model.

The ongoing SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has drawn intense focus on mathematical biology.  This area of study is now being utilized to investigate long-standing issues related to microbial epidemic modeling, with an eye toward understanding and preventing future outbreaks.  Despite the diverse nature of mathematical models being utilized in COVID-19 modeling, these models share a common underlying framework and can be examined through the lens of Bayesian statistics.  With this approach, models can be evaluated based on their underlying assumptions in light of available data, leading to more informed decisions when selecting models for forecasting and management purposes.  This process is inherently subjective, highlighting the importance of transparent communication between modelers and decision-makers to ensure that the chosen models accurately reflect their goals.  In the following sections, we will explore commonly utilized mathematical frameworks, with an emphasis on their underlying principles, before returning to the broader implications of model selection and the critical role that microbial epidemiology plays in shaping our future.

We examine the behavior of a Majorana model consisting of N spin-1/2 particles, which is then expanded to include multiple states per particle. Our investigation involves generating function methods and numerical simulations to analyze its thermodynamic properties. Unlike its bosonic counterpart, the Majorana particles exhibit an infinite specific heat as the system approaches thermal equilibrium, which can be accurately modeled using an inverse power law. We also derive a key relationship, valid for both bosons and fermions, which connects particle density to the ratio of chemical potential to temperature in a manner that is independent of the statistics governing the particles.

Acronyms are frequently encountered in technical written content, but they present a significant barrier to comprehension for readers, making them the primary focus of extensive research into Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques for their resolution. Although the role of acronyms in written communication has long been established, empirical studies examining their communication effectiveness have seldom been conducted. To introduce novel concepts and technologies to experienced professionals via the World Wide Web, content creators often rely on informal acronym resolution methods, such as capitalization and abbreviation, which may be perceived as clear by their audience. Nevertheless, further exploration is required to validate the efficacy of such practices. Our research seeks to establish an acronym resolution and disambiguation framework, considering both automatic and non-automatic approaches, ultimately presenting an experimental system named MadDog. Additionally, MadDog incorporates features enabling content creators to intentionally resolve acronyms through interactive mechanisms, including hyperlinking and semantic annotations. For evaluating the comprehension efficiency of dense web content, containing newly introduced concepts, our research also developed a task-based assessment involving actual users, which we inclusionarily discuss along with the introduction of design principles for intentional acronym resolution and further conceptual annotation.

Directly converting two-spinbose atoms into a single spin-polarized molecule through laser-induced three-body recombination is feasible, provided that certain conditions are met.  A crucial condition is that the interatomic recoil energy needs to be significantly lower than the molecular binding energy.  As an illustrative example, we show that meeting these conditions allows for the efficient transformation of two $^{87}$Rb atoms into a $^{87}$Rb2 molecule, from atoms in the $|F = 2, m_F = 2\rangle$ state.

This paper tackles a critical issue in hierarchical DNA storage systems, where maintaining high utility across multiple hierarchy levels demands effective management. Existing solutions struggle to accommodate the increased complexity caused by storage limitations in lower levels. To address this challenge, we propose a novel strategy called HADR, a method that efficiently balances the need for freshness data and structural integrity in multi-level DNA storage. By integrating directional clustering and dynamic resource allocation, HADR ensures optimal performance and operation across all hierarchy levels. Simulation results demonstrate the haptic utility of HADR in improving system-wide utility and outperforming current approaches.

Recently, research has focused on realizing two-dimensional nodal surfaces in momentum space across various types of systems, including ultra-cold atoms, photons, and sound waves. These hypersurfaces exhibit remarkable topological properties that can be manipulated through the use of band gaps and allow for efficient light localization without requiring symmetry. This work provides a concise overview of the characteristics of nodal surfaces and their recent applications, while also discussing novel concepts such as nodal points with orientation preservation, knotted trajectories in momentum space, and hyperbolic geometry implementations.

A brain tumor affects every age group and has the potential to transform healthy brain tissue into damaged area, with changes in both size and shape. MRI technology is commonly used for tumor diagnosis and planning of treatments, but interpreting this data can be challenging due to its complexity. Automated segmentation and classification techniques have been developed to simplify this process, but accurate results are difficult to achieve. In order to tackle these difficulties, a novel neural network called MAG-Net was created that handles two categories of brain tumors and segments various parts of the tumor in a single task, using MRI images. The MAG-Net network is designed to share information effectively and accurately segment the tumor by learning the relationship between different image modalities and hierarchical features. The results showed that the MAG-Net network outperformed state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy, dice similarity coefficient, and Hausdorff distance, and was particularly useful for patients due to its ability to produce consistent and reliable tumor segmentation and classification.

Differentiable ray tracing systems enable fast and precise shadow assessment.
Consequently, they can serve as powerful priors in inverse problem solutions.
However, accurately predicting shadows remains a significant difficulty.
Currently shadow models, although effective, are either overly simplistic or excessive.
We introduce a novel approach to shadow evaluation, utilizing a hybrid combination of linear optimization and differentiable rendering.
This model, free from approximations, efficiently computes complex shadows caused by object occlusions, even when light sources have large sizes.
The model also determines the precise light loss at the target object and outputs the shadow specifically, not the occluded area.
The differentiable component leverages modern rendering technologies for superior performance, specifically, we achieve 10 times faster evaluation per frame compared to a baseline system.
The model demonstrates exceptionally accurate shadows in our benchmarks, outperforming alternatives by a substantial margin of 0.05 RMSE.
Code is accessible on GitHub.

A significant challenge in the realm of video analysis arises from insufficient frame rates, which frequently occurs in real-world scenarios and substantially affects the accuracy of subsequent tasks such as segmentation and motion estimation. The primary issue with existing high-frame-rate enhancement methods, including interpolation between adjacent frames, lies in the creation of severe interlacing artifacts, ghosting effects, and frame halos. These methods also result in frames that are temporally inconsistent. To address these deficiencies, we propose a groundbreaking approach called Instantaneous Deep Video Deinterlacing, also known as IDVI, which processes each interlaced frame independently, allowing for processing between 30 and 60 times faster than adjacent-frame techniques, while outperforming them by up to 8 times in accuracy. The core of our IDVI approach involves learning three distinct but interconnected components: an instantaneous interpolation that fills the missing half of the frame, an instantaneous scanning transformation, and an instantaneous motion estimation allowing each half-frame to be accurately represented and analyzed.

To examine the shape of nuclear distributions, it's crucial to consider not just the radius but also higher-order parameters that provide a comprehensive description. In a study, we calculated the root-mean-square radius of the neutron distribution across 50 stable nuclei, utilizing three widely accepted relativistic non-relativistic average field models.
