By smoothly modifying the treatment modalities for minimal loss consistency, our method leads to more accurate segmentations. Experimental evaluations with limited labeled data have demonstrated the efficacy of our proposed technique, yielding substantial improvements when applied in combination with other methods. Additionally, results indicate that modalities-transformed fusions provide nearly dual-modal performance with minimal modalities.

The ATLAS Jet Trigger System on the ATLAS detector at the LHC needs to enhance its throughput capacity to fully explore Higher Luminosity Operations at the LHC. Due to its present implementation's limited processing speed and excessive system complexity, upgrading the hardware is essential. The proposed solution involves a new hardware component called the Local Front-End Processor (LEFP), which employs an Intel Xeon Phi processor to efficiently handle real-time data processing and communication between components. The proposed system utilizes a single ultra-scale processor to replace multiple conventional processors, thereby reducing system complexity while maintaining high-velocity data processing capabilities. Benchmark tests indicate that the ULTRA-LEFP solution outperforms its conventional counterpart in speed and efficiency, requiring significantly less power while providing similar or superior performance. Furthermore, compatibility with the existing system protocol has been demonstrated through successful communication tests.

This paper presents a novel framework called ANR (Articulated Neural Rendering), which effictively addresses the challenge of realistic visualization for one's own identity in a virtual environment. ANR enhances traditional neural rendering techniques by incorporating a set of deformable neural components that complement the primary scene representation. These components are strategically placed in a hierarchical bone tree to enhance accuracy and smoothness. By integrating ANR's components into a coherent model, we achieve highly lifelike images and smooth animations. Notably, ANR is particularly advantageous for applications requiring virtual avatars and selfvisualization. Virtual try-on and selfvisualization are two such applications, which ANR tackles by effectively handling complex deformations. ANR is an innovative approach that provides a seamless and accurate avatar experience.

A fundamental characteristics of chaotic systems is their sensitivity to starting conditions, which has significant implications for machine learning applications. In this study, we designed and tested multiple graph neural network models to learn chaos from experimental data and analyzed how they measure sensitivity to starting conditions. These models were applied to two examples of chaos: a graph-based Poincaré map and an experiment on a quantum chaotic system. The analysis of their attention mechanisms provided insights into how machine learning algorithms analyze and prioritize information, which could help bridge the gap between data-driven and theory-based approaches in several areas of research, including physics and the social sciences.

Knowledge tracing has emerged as a cutting-edge learning technology that
automatically evaluates students' evolving mastery of subject matter.
Despite its success, a major barrier to entry for new research in this field
has been the lack of unified evaluation benchmarks. To address this challenge,
we have developed PyKT, a comprehensive Python benchmarking framework for
knowledge tracing. PyKT offers a transparent and accessible platform for
researchers to compare and contrast different knowledge tracing models in a
transparent and accessible manner. By leveraging PyKT, researchers can more easily
access and evaluate their models using a standardised set of datasets and
metrics, thereby reducing the associated experimentation costs.

Given a smooth, non-compact manifold $M$, we demonstrate that the closure of elliptic operators comprises the set of all SO($m$)- and $\mathbb{R}$-irreducible representations that appear in $L^2(M)$. This result extends to any non-compact algebraic variety $X$, where we obtain the closure of elliptic representations as the set of all irreducible $\mathbb{R}$-representations occurring in $L^2(X)$.

This paper introduces Alethe, a high-level language for structuring solver proofs, which can be efficiently translated into ConfPro's final form. A translation into the downstream proof system is proposed, with the aim of making other proofs more comprehensible to humans. This makes it possible for various proof systems to seamlessly utilize the outputs from modern SMT solvers.

Using buffered asynchronous techniques has been previously incorporated into federated learning to prevent asynchronous delays and communication bandwidth limitations. These methods prevent later input data from overwriting earlier data by accumulating the information in a buffer. The buffer is periodically utilized in standard federated learning rounds when necessary servers are located. Although the inclusion of the buffer provides a larger dataset, it also introduces a discrepancy between training and test distributions, potentially increasing the variance of gradient descent and undermining the benefits of processing a larger batch size. To mitigate these issues, the paper proposes a straightforward method for relaxing the constraint of unconstrained gradients in federated learning. By allowing later data to overwrite earlier data in a buffer, the proposal ensures that the training and testing distributions are more closely aligned. The approach is evaluated in a preliminary experimental setup involving the implementation of the proposed method alongside the standard buffered asynchronous federated learning protocol on the MNIST dataset.

This work focuses on a cutting-edge ASR approach, known as "Rough-To-Fine", and calls it out for its intriguing use of low-level details. We also put this approach on par with other techniques and conduct extensive testing across different language scenarios. Moreover, the work goes beyond English, exploring and validating the rough-to-fine approach on other languages. The work also involves a unique cross-language ASR transfer, involving training models at a noisy English level and assessing their performance on a cleaner English language and two different German languages, namely Standard and dialectal accents. The result of this experiment yields a surprising discovery that the rough-to-fine approach achieves the best outcomes in this cross-language setting.

The popularity of professional esports has created a significant interest in analyzing player team dynamics. Representing graph neural networks (GNNs) and node embedding techniques has received substantial research attention due to their potential applications in coaching and player marketing. However, a high-quality dataset is lacking to accurately evaluate the performance of these node representation methods that preserve graph structure and role-based information. We propose two diverse datasets, including Twitch teams, which closely mirror real-world sports team compositions, to fill this gap. Twitch teams represent a community where gamers gain fame through live streaming and frequently compete together in tournaments. We collected historical data on player memberships and team structures from the early 2010s to 2020. Thorough representations were assessed on both datasets, including node embeddings for various graph neural network models and basic methods like Laplacian Smoothed and Spectral Convoluted. A high level of similarity between past and future player team memberships indicates strong performance of the representations, while clustering algorithms were employed to investigate the role-based aspects. We hope that these datasets will help accelerate research into graph structure and role-based node representations that can be applied to coaching and business purposes.

Our study reveals that previous research on the $B$ meson decay form factors around 1.5 TeV has been hindered by the lack of sufficient data. To overcome this limitation, we've compiled more comprehensive data by analyzing the $\pi^+\pi^-$ and $K^+K^-$ invariant mass spectra from $B^0\to \pi^0\pi^0$, $B^+ \to \pi^+ \pi^-$ and $B^0 \to K^+ K^-$ decays. Additionally, we've identified and removed the effect of the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance, allowing for a more accurate analysis. This enables us to estimate the potential contribution of the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance in the $B$ meson form factors. Our findings suggest that the potential contribution of the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance in the $B$ meson form factors is minimal, accounting for less than 5%. This outcome implies that the $B$ meson form factors derived from time-dependent asymmetry measurements may overestimate the actual magnitude of the form factors.

If the Dark Matter consists of the portion that's separated from the Standard Model and constitutes the "Shadow Dimension", a significant part of the Primordial Black Holes would also be isolated from the Standard Model and reside in distinct dimensional planes. This means that Black Holes interacting only through gravity could constitute the Dark Matter, and as a result, we can anticipate observing signs of Primordial Black Holes merging via gravitational waves from future sensitive detectors like LISA, Taiji, and CFGEC.

However, the hypothesis suggesting the Dark Matter is comprised of the Shadow Dimension faces the Challenge of the Swampland, proposing the existence of at least one more dimension beyond the Shadow Dimension and its corresponding physical laws. This would imply the existence of Dark Gauge Fields within that additional dimension, and since Black Holes emit such fields during the Hawking Radiation Phase, Dark Matter composed of Primordial Black Holes should exhibit differences in evaporation rates and masses. Similarly, Dark Matter composed of WIMPs, which constitute such fields, could be produced through the Schwinger Effect in those fields, and this process might create imbalances between matter and antimatter that we can detect in form of Dark Matter's antimatter counterparts.

Force control systems with series elastic actuators are highly beneficial for collaborative robots due to their safety and performance capabilities. By utilizing a simple, high-stiffness elastic transmission in the actuator, these systems can achieve precise force control through an advanced observer called SEA-SFA. The proposed approach effectively overcomes the limitations of traditional high-pass filters used to process the elastic force signal, which often distort the control signal and limit performance. The closed-loop system's capability to track desired trajectories and reject external disturbances is enhanced by eliminating this restrictive constraint. Furthermore, the system's ability to follow low-frequency sine wave trajectories and reject band-pass disturbances is improved, demonstrating the benefits of using the newly developed elastic force signal processing method.

Liquid crystal mixtures that are held between two parallel plates can be analogized to biological structures, such as epithelial cells that are aligned and adhere to one another. When these liquids, specifically nematic lipids, are mixed with fatty acid glycerol triesters that have a plate-like structure, they can be compared to biological membranes. By observing the behavior of these mixtures under a microscope at low magnification, we can study how the liquid crystal affects the fatty acid glycerol triesters and potentially lead to material failures. In our research, we studied the point at which these materials may fail, also referred to as fracture, and found that the surrounding liquid crystal has a directed preference in which the separation occurs. We discovered that fractures tend to propagate more easily in certain directions and that the properties of the surrounding mixture can be used to predict the strength of the materials. A significant finding in our research is the correlation between the material properties and the threshold at which the fracture occurs, which can be used to predict the strength of the surrounding mixture at a specific angle.

This study explores a range of 3D SU(Nc) lattice gauge theories that include various types of scalar fields and interact with them through specific potentials. By examining the lattice models' phase charts, research reveals the existence of distinct Higgs states corresponding to each scalar field, as well as an important transition between these states when the SU(Nf) symmetry is unbroken. This transition displays characteristics typical of the crossover seen in QCD.

Achieving autonomous navigation for underwater robots without human supervision is challenging due to limited and unreliable sensor data.  One promising approach involves using Gaussian processes to model sensor data, allowing the robot to learn from unlabelled data and account for time-varying sensations.  Despite the success of this approach in previous studies, training sparse Gaussian processes on time-varying data remains an open problem due to the dynamic changes in the sparse data.  Although the relationship between time and the parameters of the Gaussian process could potentially be modeled using a regularizer, this approach often results in inaccurate sensations and unnecessary computational costs when using third-order or higher splines.  As an alternative, we propose a two-step approach: initially, the robot narrows down the region of interest using a basic Gaussian process with a single time prior, and then gathers rich data within this region; subsequently, the sparse Gaussian process is retrained, leveraging the reduced data requirements due to the confined region.

We study the minimum depth arrangement network with linear-size comparators, specifically at O(n) comparators, and discover variations of classic arrangement networks like Benes network and Omega network. However, our research reveals networks with lower depth alternatives at 2log^1/2_2(n)+15 stages, aiding hardware designs of sorting networks with reduced depth. Our improvements significantly decrease the calculated minimum lower bounds from 2.8log_2(n)-5.6 to 2.45log^1/2_2(n)+10.5, demonstrating novel networks with stage counts matching the updated bound for values of n between 2^10 and 2^20.

We examine a nonisotropic dual-fluid stellar object within the framework of General Relativity, employing a polytropic equation of state for both its longitudinal and transverse pressures, which differ from each other, and we derive conditions ensuring the stability of such a system, utilizing the bounded rate of change test and the surface behavior test, and we also investigate the causal propagation of both fluids, and we further establish that the speed of both pressures does not exceed the speed of light, and we also derive necessary conditions for the smooth matching of the interior metric with the exterior Schwarzschild metric at the boundary of the star, and we further illustrate these theoretical concepts through a specific model and relevant physical parameters for compact stars.

We've used high-quality, recent data to create a set of galaxy models that resemble the Milky Way. By analyzing the rotation curves and stellar density distributions of these models, we've determined how the spiral structure in our own galaxy and others may be oriented. Considering the orientation distributions of the Milky Way and several similar galaxies from the Milky Way-Andromeda fall-out, we've established the most likely orientations for both in a comparative study. Furthermore, we explored whether the intrinsic symmetries of these galaxies could explain the observed rotation of their spiral arms by analyzing the inclinations of their arms individually or collectively. However, these methods yielded inconsistent results. Therefore, custom-made potential fields will be necessary to understand the 3D geometry of the Milky Way in future research.

Galactic mergers and amalgamations are key processes that facilitate the formation of large galaxies within the $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model. This paper examines the impact of magnetic fields on galaxy mergers by conducting high-resolution simulations of disk galaxies and analyzing magnetic field interactions with other components. Researchers used these simulations to investigate the role of magnetic fields in shaping gas and stellar disks, taking into account various factors including magnetic field strength and viscosity. Findings show that weak magnetic fields have a negligible impact on merged galaxies, whereas stronger fields can lead to more distinct morphological differences. Furthermore, moderate levels of turbulence induced by magnetic fields result in similar outcomes to those produced by higher levels of turbulence induced by other components. Ultimately, galaxy mergers amplify magnetic fields and contribute to the generation of moderate-$z$ MRK spectra commonly associated with large galaxies.

Identifying severe COVID-19 infections through chest CT images is a crucial step in managing the pandemic with limited labeled data for severe cases, we propose a novel approach called Infection-aware Contrastive Mixup Classification (ICMC).ICMC leverages contrastive learning to preserve low-level features and a dynamic loss function to guide the contrastive aspect of the network, it also prevents feature leakage during the training process.Moreover, we introduce a new data augmentation technique called global local feature mixup (GLFM), which fuses adjacent images to create artificial healthy CT samples, it is particularly useful in enhancing the contrastive component of the network, it allows the model to learn the characteristic curves of pulmonary vessels found in healthy lungs, we integrate our proposed ICRC and GLFM into the existing framework and it significantly enhances the performance of COVID-19 severity classification through comprehensive experiments conducted on a real-world dataset, our results demonstrate substantial improvements in accuracy compared to the baseline and other advanced methods, it reduces the accuracy gap with the current state-of-the-art method and our refined approach achieves the highest accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, it surpassing the existing infection-aware classification baseline by 6% and the basic 4-way CT classifier by 2%.

Most current systems for correcting grammatical errors rely heavily on large amounts of annotated data within a specific domain. The requirement for extensively labeled datasets impedes the development of general-purpose error correction tools sensitive to various domains. The limitations of fully supervised approaches prompt the investigation of extra-data techniques to enhance performance on unfamiliar domains, specifically focusing on graphically error correction (GER). Through the application of graphically error correction tasks to known domains, the results show that active learning and transfer learning methods fall short in achieving satisfactory graphically error correction performance on new domains, however, the data selection strategies are then replaced with a multi-shot graphically error transfer framework based on neural networks. The outcomes of the experiment, conducted on the main categories of the IEEE Data Portals dataset, reveal that both the active learning and the low-data transfer learning methods underperform relative to the proposed meta-learning approach, which demonstrates a significant improvement in F-score by +24% compared to the baseline system, indicating the potential of the graphically error transfer approach to attain competitive perfomance on novel domains with relatively limited labeled data.

This research paper develops a statistical statistical ambiguity model to accurately reflect the uncertainty behind using rounded numerical data for calculating totals and averages. Specifically, it focuses on scenarios where a mean of a set of hidden values is presented as an integer after rounding, which has broader applications, including privacy-preserving data analysis and statistical estimation of totals from averaged information. By formulating an ambiguity set, we can arrive at tight upper and lower bounds for unspecified individual values. These bounds can be utilized to: determine the feasible range for each unknown value, assess the probability of each value occurring, and answer linear questions about the hidden values. We illustrate how these techniques can help resolve ambiguity in a real-world dataset.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic structure of a centered honeycomb antiferromagnetic material, GdInO$_3$, as a thin film and in bulk form. Examination was carried out using X-ray diffraction, energy-dispersive spectroscopy, and further magnetic analysis through muon-spin relaxation and susceptibility measurements. These studies revealed two distinct magnetic transitions at notable temperatures: one at the Néel temperature (TN) of 16.2 K and another at (T2) 4.5 K. Furthermore, magnetic susceptibility and energy-dispersive spectroscopy confirmed that this material maintains its antiferromagnetic order even under an applied external magnetic field.

We are examining the creation of local, decentralized mechanisms to facilitate the allocation of non-transferable items to agents who may act strategically, with the goal of establishing efficient and equitable equilibria. In our analysis, we consider two common scenarios for valuations: first, where agents assign the same value to each item, and second, where agents value each item differently. For additive valuations, we discover that no strategy-proof mechanism exists that could produce efficient outcomes even for two agents desiring one item each. On the other hand, we discover that there is a mechanism capable of supporting a Pare-optimal equilibrium among agents with substitutable demands, and we establish that this equilibrium is not efficient for free-goods scenarios. Lastly, we investigate the impact of transfers on Nash equilibria and establish that there is a polynomial-sized support Nash equilibrium with an efficient outcome for two agents with unit-demand and symmetric additive valuation profiles, and this equilibrium holds for unit-demand agents with valuations that value objects no less than they value them.

The concept of deterministic domain adaptation, a well-established framework, implies that every pixel in a source image maps to a specific target image pixel under the same domain transformation. Previous research focused heavily on deterministic domain adaptation but neglected the underlying assumption of uniqueness. Our study challenges this assumption by introducing the broader framework of stochastic domain adaptation. We theoretically explore stochastic domain adaptation and demonstrate its connection to source-based data, which is widely used for unsupervised image denoising and color correction. This research ultimately paves the way for more flexible and diverse domain adaptations.

The spiral galaxy UGC 8839 exhibits an unusually high inclination and a substantial hydrogen mass, leading to its classification as a hyper-lobed galaxy. Our in-depth analysis using optical and radio data along with NASA-DSS color imagery sheds new light on this rare celestial body. We uncovered a highly distinct, gas-rich disk rotating at a constant speed, almost perpendicular to the galaxy's axis. This discovery is unprecedented and offers new insights into the evolution of gas-rich disk galaxies. The superposed spiral patterns appear well-defined outside the galaxy's core, which exhibits unusually low surface brightness when compared to its mass. This discrepancy is likely attributed to a massive, gas-rich disk positioned behind the visible stellar component. If fully accounted for, this discovery would elevate the galaxy's hydrogen mass estimate by a factor of four. Further observations of UCGC 8839 may help explain the formation and evolution of gas-rich disk galaxies and aid in accounting for the missing biomass in the galaxy's hydrogen mass budget.

This paper reviews current research on paleo-detectors, which are sensors made from ancient rock that has been cooled below a critical temperature and contains natural radioactive gas. The detectors offer enhanced sensitivity to dark matter due to the already existing preparation and inclusion of potassium-40 as a reference for other isotopes, such as arsenic-73, aluminum-27, and silicon-28. The review covers various methods of exposing the paleo-detectors to dark matter interaction studies, such as using the detectors as part of surface or underground experiments, as well as deep paleo-detectors in astro-paleo-neutrino observatories. The review also discusses strategies for increasing exposure through inclined exposures, underground labs, and the use of different types of rocks, as well as identifying challenges and the need for new types of detectors with higher sensitivity and low contamination. The research has the potential to either rule out or confirm WIMP models and, in the case of finding dark matter, allow for isotopic analysis that could lead to a more thorough understanding of its properties.

This paper introduces DP-Sync, which incorporates differential privacy into real-time secure outsourcing scenarios, enabling a server to store large datasets while a client accesses and manipulates data, with the client's help. By utilizing a novel scheme based on fully homomorphic encryption and a differential privacy-based update pattern concealment strategy through a private channel, DP-Sync permits the client to perform search, range query, update, and deletion operations, allowing the data to stay current. Moreover, DP-Sync automatically creates the private data set from raw data and ensures differential privacy against a malicious server, albeit with some efficiency implications.

Decision tree-based machine learning models are capable of providing feature significance ranking, which can be utilized to guide expert input and perform adversarial assessments. However, these models are susceptible to overestimating the importance of deceptive features that can be exploited by adversaries. As a result, their reliability relies on the attack method employed. In contrast, methods like Multi-Uncertainty-minimization Cross-entropy (MUC) which combine cross-entropy loss reduction with uncertainty control have been shown to not only enhance classification accuracy but also offer reliable feature importance assessment. This study integrates MUC by utilizing its entropy-based metric to design a decision tree-based attack and proposes using Adversarial Evaluation (AE) with Random Forest (RRF) and combining it with MUC (MUC-rRF) as an alternative to decision tree-based adversarial evaluation. Our results show that the MUC-rRF model surpasses random forest and supports the hypothesis that entropy-based assessment outperforms probability ranking in evaluating feature significance. Furthermore, the MUC-rRF model exhibits greater susceptibility to decision tree-based evaluation than AE-rRF, which implies that decision tree models may be prone to yielding misleading adversarial evaluations of certain deceptive features that RRF or MUC-rRF could correctly identify.

Minimally invasive surgery has emerged as a highly effective treatment, enabling high success and low complication rates. However, the procedure involves high risks and costs, necessifying advanced training for medical professionals. One promising approach is computer-assisted surgery, a field yet to be widely adopted due to challenges such as real-time surgical instrument segmentation. These instruments are crucial to identify and track during the surgical procedure. Current methods for detecting and locating objects have proven effective but often struggle with real-time processing of high-resolution surgical videos. Over-segmentation and under-segmentation are among the issues encountered with existing approaches due to the high frame rate and complex background of medical videos. Various methods, including fully connected convolutional networks, R-CNNs, and single shot multi-box detectors, have been developed but fall short of providing a highly efficient solution. Numerous frameworks such as Fast R-CNN, FASTER R-CNN, and mask R-CNN have been utilized but often result in over-shoot and low frame rates. Numerous methods such as NToM and UNET have been developed but often result in low frame rates and high computation times. Various methods such as fully connected high-level networks and mask R-CNN have been developed but often result in low frame rates and incomplete segmentation. This research explores an innovative instrument segmentation method that achieves precise mask segmentation, incomplete segmentation, low frame rates, and incomplete detection and location. Numerous techniques such as single shot multi-box detector and mask R-CNN have been developed

One of the most significant tasks in the field of individual re-identification is developing new datasets to re-identify people. In order to create high-quality data for this purpose, several key aspects need to be considered: a large and diverse set of individuals, a wide range of image perspectives and lighting conditions, and a compelling and balanced training and testing configuration. In order to evaluate and assess new re-identification datasets, unsupervised methods are commonly employed. However, these approaches are limited by their reliance on pre-existing datasets and their inability to accurately measure performance on larger scales. To address these shortcomings, we propose a novel and comprehensive framework for unsupervised individual re-identification that utilizes contrastive learning to analyze the visual features of people and their contexts. Our method, which incorporates a variety of pre-trained image encoding networks and employs a negative pair sampling strategy, enables a thorough evaluation of re-identification datasets under diverse conditions and yields state-of-the-art results, even without the use of identity-specific annotation.

This paper presents a novel practice-oriented approach to hazard rate prediction in financial time series, utilizing the actual threshold modeling of GARCH models. We developed a unique method to estimate the actual threshold of GARCH models through a combination of scale transformations and the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm. A case study with DAX data demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach in hazard rate prediction, outperforming traditional methods such as Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall. As actual threshold GARCH models are commonly used in industry for risk measurement, our model contributes to the assessment of risk models' reliability and validity. By providing a framework for the critical parameter estimation of GARCH models, it allows for the examination of risks associated with model misspecification.

The discovery of multiple millisecond pulsars has enabled precise measurements of fundamental constants and gravitational phenomena. Determining the stability of these constants and the behavior of general relativity relies heavily on the accuracy of involved parameters. By analyzing data from three well-studied pulsar systems, we have derived new upper limits for the amplitude of stochastic gravity waves and the strain of linear gravitational waves, which in turn has implications for the population of these waves in the universe.

Our calculation of the correlation function between flavor-specific pion operators within chiral perturbation theory reveals a discrepancy with certain lattice QCD results. This discrepancy persists even when considering one-pion exchange contributions to the two-flavor correlation function, suggesting the possibility of higher-order contributions being significant. This finding has potential implications for the reliability of chiral perturbation theory at the scale typically employed for determining the light quark mass.

To understand how angular momentum in protostars is removed, we need to examine the behavior of accretion rates and current models suggest high variability. However, there is very little observed support for this required fluctuation because observed outbursts in planetary formation stars show significant variability but not to the extent required. By examining high-cadence data from three protostars and, specifically, XX Cha in detail, we found extreme and periodic variability in optical brightness, corresponding to an order-of-magnitude variation in accretion rate and activity level. By considering this finding along with previous results (Penellope and Penellope I), we concluded that the necessary condition for this process may be driven by magnetic fluctuations on short timescales that are not audible in optical brightness variations in most cases. Consequently, the large dispersion in observed accretion rates and the rates seen in individual disks are not entirely surprising.

This study explores the concept of inequity of chance and its impact on income reallocation. We define the opportunity inequality measure and its properties, including a specific norm, and derive its connection to a semi-variance difference approach. We then investigate the characteristics of opportunity inequality using a variance function and confirm these features through numerical results. The study delves into the criteria that preserve opportunity inequality and identifies a class of equity taxes based on a majorization relationship. The paper also considers income data sorted by chance inequality and examines the effects of various operations, such as swapping, cutting, and blending on the opportunity inequality index. We then apply these theoretical findings to an empirical dataset, presenting descriptive statistics and an analysis of income reallocation through a simulation using the AF class. Additionally, the study compares the opportunity inequality among U.S. states and distinguishes their chance inequality patterns.

Given a pair of Borel subalgebras of a simple algebraic group, we keep the standard basis and modify the quantum product in (classical) K theory by the diagonal operation, then derive how the relations change when moving to a specific path in the Grassmannian of Borel pairs. This process results in formulas for the modified k-Bernoulli operators that apply to Grassmannians, flag varieties, and other varieties like the Lagrangian Grassmannian, orthogonal flag variety, and the symplectic flag variety.

The vast use of automated machine learning pipelines has greatly improved the efficiency of the process, but identifying and addressing data issues remains a major troubleshooting challenge. Traditionally, manual data inspection has been the main approach, which is time-consuming and labor-intensive. This paper proposes a novel method to automatically identify data problems contributing to suboptimal pipeline performance using Shapley values. A tool called S3ML has been developed to apply our technique to multiple linearization methods, specifically Union-Infinitely Infinitesimal Marginal Contribution, Kernel-Linkage Learning and Gradient-Weighted. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets have demonstrated the superiority of S3ML in pinpointing data issues, its method can be easily adapted to automatically generate data corrections to optimize pipeline output.

This month's MAVERIC Science Update features recent findings from the MAVERIC project on a topic in Galactic globular clusters. The MAVERIC team has been investigating the radio and gamma-ray phenomena within the Milky Way's globular clusters using a combination of data analysis and high-cadence simulations of cataclysmic variables. Their work has revealed significant discoveries regarding the dynamic nature of X-ray binary systems that power these clusters' central sources. Through a statistical model called Liac-C, the MAVERIC team has established that the merger rate of these binary systems follows the dynamic origin theory and holds true when observed both within and beyond the Milky Way, providing crucial insight into the source of these cosmic phenomena.

We propose an innovative approach to restoring corrupted hypergraphs, emphasizing the benefit of given cutsets on reconstruction accuracy. The primary challenge in restoring corrupted hypergraphs stems from the fact that the removal of hyperedges fragments data and leads to multiple pieces. The proposed method utilizes a cutting guidance network that determines the cost of connecting each pair of nodes, based on the available cutsets. By employing a hyperedge prediction network, we can recover the corrupted hypergraph. The prediction network is guided by the cost calculated from the cutsets using the cutting guidance network. The proposed method can be viewed as the integration of two models: a hyperedge prediction model similar to those used in homogeneous data scenarios and a guidance model that operates on bipartite data. The proposed approach leverages the cutting guidance network to directly learn the cost function that maximizes the information theory-based objective. The proposed method demonstrates a significant improvement in performance compared to the baseline models on synthetic and real-world datasets.

We propose an optimized power distribution formula for directional emissions from a microcavity laser, employing a novel entropic gauge, and prove its universality. Additionally, we demonstrate that the entropic approach simplifies derivation of the linear rate equations, yielding a closed-form solution and an explicit connection between the entropic emission and the quasi Fermi energy of the quasi-equilibrium photon gas. This equality can also be derived from traditional maximum entropy methods, showcasing the superiority of our approach in clarity, conciseness, and universality over conventional methods.

The spectroscopic analysis of thermal atomic ensembles illuminated by incoherent light involves examining both self-emitted radiation and reflected light. In a detailed study of one-dimensional alkali metal atoms such as Rb and Cs, we derived analytical expressions for the second-order correlation function. These expressions account for collective effects and can be numerically evaluated to visualize the underlying phenomena. Our calculations show that superradiance leads to enhanced two-photon emissions, while increased atomic temperature due to photon-driven thermalization results in a decline in two-photon correlations. The magnitude of this effect is significant, particularly at higher temperatures where it dominates. This investigation serves as the first theoretical foundation for measuring two-photon correlations experimentally and may have significant implications for quantum communications systems utilizing atomic ensembles as memory devices or sensor arrays in magnetometry.

Offline learning and training for multiple interacting agents is a crucial yet difficult challenge. It becomes even more complicated with an increase in the number of involved agents. Off-line training typically relies on labeled interactions, yet there's often insufficient useful information in the data as not all recorded interactions between agents show the positive outcomes needed for effective training. This problem is particularly accentuated in multi-agent settings, where the lack of sufficient valuable data severely hinders online learning as well. This research focuses particularly on the offline learning and training of multiple interacting agents. It suggests novel methods to both efficiently utilize the limited available data and manage the complexities arising from the interactions between the agents. It suggests both a method to adapt the action space in Contract Deep Q-Learning (CDQL) for continuous agents and an method to generate synthetic transitions in Graph Convolutional Network based Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (GCN-OFF-MARL) for discrete agents. It utilized the proposed methods on the Mountain Car and Multi-car Traffic Jam problems, with substantial improvements demonstrated in the results.

We developed a novel approach for aligning megavoltage images, utilizing a combination of a 2D alignment and a 3D deformation, tailored for robust胃癌 treatment. By training a convolutional neural network to predict the optimal 2D/3D alignment and the deformation, we demonstrated this method could account for both predictable internal movements and organ shifts, largely eliminating the need for manual image registration. Furthermore, when working with aligned images, our network was capable of directly estimating the tumor volume, even when only given a single kilovoltage image as input. This direct end-to-end approach yielded slightly more accurate results than a baseline network that worked with manually registered images. Notably, when comparing this to previously used methods that involved multiple sequential steps and transformations, our simplified process using the aligned images resulted in a significant reduction in overall error.

We investigate single-particle entanglement in spatially entangled states, which can exhibit nonlocal correlations when measured at distant locations. Single-particle entanglement implies the ability to perform teleportation and generate nonlocal correlations through measure-and-superdense coding. Notably, we find that single-particle entanglement allows for an asymmetric generation of nonlocal correlations, a phenomenon known as single-particle steering. This effect emerges from the use of localized measurements rather than a specific type of measurement, and we provide a measure to quantify single-particle steering. Furthermore, we investigate its relationship with other forms of nonlocal correlations and introduce an entanglement inequality that is connected to it. This entanglement inequality can be violated by coherent states in a locally rotated cat state (LRCAS), and we demonstrate that measuring these states leads to single-particle steering. Consequently, our work reveals that single-particle entanglement can give rise to genuine nonlocal effects like single-particle steering.

This paper explores a Federated Learning framework incorporating Blockchain technology to support autonomous vehicles in the Internet of Vehicles. Machine Learning models in IoVs face privacy concerns and data manipulation risks, which can be mitigated through a Federated Learning approach that trains models on local data and shares only model updates. However, existing FL methods have drawbacks such as compromised security, trust issues, and unknown contributing nodes. Introducing Blockchain technology to the FL framework offers a potential solution by providing transparency, immutability, and traceability to the model sharing process, although there are challenges such as computational demands and data size. This paper delves into the potential of a Blockchain-supported FL framework for IoVs, highlights suitable consensus mechanisms and Blockchain platforms, and offers design considerations for the framework's implementation.

V392 Persei, the most recent dwarf nova outburst since 1891, caught our attention during its normal brightness phase in May 2021. In-depth observations from the Fermi-LAT and HESS telescopes during the outburst in 2021 revealed unusually high levels of \gamma-ray emission compared to other recorded outbursts. V392's \gamma-ray emission appeared to originate from the nova outburst, yet its underlying binary system is still capable of generating high-energy particles. V392's outburst in 2021 is unlike previous ones, such as in 1937 and 1891, which were too dim to be seen without a telescope. V392's system has been accumulating material on its white dwarf accretion disk until it reached a critical mass, triggering a dwarf nova outburst.

To maintain robust and scalable quantum memory, it's necessary to perform accurate one and multi-qubit operations on entangled qubits. Within the context of the toric code, we examined the error rates for local operations on isolated pairs of qubits, and compared them to those on larger groups of non-interacting qubits. We found that, when the code distance increases, the error rates for the two-qubit operation behave differently from the multi-qubit operation, specifically showing saturation at certain distances. This outcome suggests that, in order to gain the full memory capacity of the toric code, it's crucial to minimize leaks occurring during quantum operations, specifically targeting operations that involve the largest possible number of qubits.

A novel approach is proposed for creating an optimized codebook and encoding feedback effectively, addressing the limitations of existing methods that rely on arbitrary selection. Traditional methods, including grid search and Gaussian mixture model, result in suboptimal matching between precursors and codebooks. Our method involves training a GMM using a random set of magnetic resonance images, followed by a feedback process using maximum a posteriori encoding. This ensures each precursor is associated with a specific codebook entry. The proposed method's performance is equivalent to semi-blind source separation methods, offering a more efficient feedback encoding process. Unlike existing techniques, our approach does not necessitate codebook optimization, instead utilizing the codebook's inherent structure for effective feedback encoding. This method is particularly suited for the use of commercial off-the-shelf sequences, ensuring an equivalent solution to certain advanced techniques, but with a more feasible feedback encoding process. Our proposed method is well-suited for implementation in FDD systems.

A robust, magnetic-field-induced supersonic wind blows perpendicularly across a 2D plane, 
which arises from the nonequilibrium Hofstadter model and maintains its speed 
regardless of the magnetic field's strength. This wind corresponds to an angular momentum 
flow that can be measured using Ginzburg-Landau vortices. We verify this phenomenon 
using a 2D superconducting circuit model and provide a clear explanation for its 
existence in terms of anomalous edge states. These states result from the breakdown of 
local thermodynamic equilibrium and give the system unique properties differentiating it 
from equilibrium systems.

The theory of bondi mass loss due to gravitational wave radiation has long been known, but its quantum counterpart remains unclear. This work compares the classical and quantum limits for the mass loss rate in the bondi framework, accounting for gravitational wave and photon emission. Our analysis employs the wave equation in flat spacetime and confirms that, in a large class of scenarios, the quantum and classical results are consistent. However, it also identifies specific scenarios where they diverge. These discrepancies may be linked to the properties of solutions in flat spacetime and could hold significance beyond this study.

We plan to examine the unique environment of nuclear star clusters by comparing them to field clusters. While the extreme conditions of nuclear star clusters have already been studied theoretically, a statistical analysis of these clusters has not yet been conducted. This analysis would help us better understand the cosmic evolution of cluster systems and provide a foundation for future observational studies. To achieve this, we have derived a theoretical framework for predicting the gravitational wave background produced by primordial stars in nuclear star clusters, and compared it to the stochastic gravitational wave background arising from field clusters. Our findings indicate that the gravitational wave background from primordial stars in nuclear star clusters may contribute significantly to the overall background, particularly in the frequency range detectable by fourth-generation gravitational wave detectors. This underscores the importance of studying nuclear star clusters not only for our understanding of the cluster itself but also for its potential contribution to the overall gravitational wave background.

The first-generation Chinese Gamma-Ray Experiment aboard a satellite (GECAM) is specially designed to study high-energy bursts, known as Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs). GECAM consists of two small satellites, each equipped with four high-sensitivity gamma-ray detectors called Gamma-Ray Ballistometers (GBAs). These detectors are composed of multiple layers of small spheres made of Terfella-Lessing (TLL) material. A detailed analysis was conducted to evaluate GECAM's performance in detecting GRBs, using data from the first-generation satellites during their operational period from May 2018 to the present. By analyzing the energy spectra of GRBs recorded by the satellites and comparing them to the average background spectra collected by the GBAs, a grand simulation (GSS) of GECAM's response to GRBs was created. The comparison between the GSS and actual GECAM data showed a high level of consistency, indicating that the simulation parameters accurately reflect the satellites' performance in detecting GRBs. This research also highlights the importance of accurately modeling the TLL material used in GECAM to improve GRB detection and suggests that future single-detector missions could benefit from running live data through a simplified version of the GSS to accurately estimate the observed energy spectra of GRBs.

This article investigates the semigroup of operators on BMOA-type spaces, denoted as $BMOA(p,q,s)$, where the notation $BMOA(p,q,s)$ is used for certain Minkowski-type spaces of analytic functions in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$. Specifically, we examine the semigroup of analytic functions $ \mathcal{A} \subseteq BMOA(p,q,s)$ by analyzing its associated infinitesimal generator and determining which subgroups of $\mathcal{A}$ preserve the structure of $BMOA(p,q,s)$ by using the Szeg{\"o} projection method. Furthermore, we investigate the representation of the Beurling–Naimark projection on $BMOA(p,q,s)$ and determine the continuity of both the Szeg{\"o} projection and canonical dual pair operators on this space, before focusing on Laguerre–Szeg{\"o} operators and their relationship to Hankel operators and composition semigroups of operators on $BMOA(p,q,s)$.

It is widely assumed that modern research articles are devoid of reading enjoyment and effective knowledge sharing, yet this common belief requires validation. A novel approach is introduced to quantify the information and readability levels of scientific literature, which is otherwise abstract. It employs a combination of natural language processing and content analysis techniques to assess the complexity of language used, as well as content mining and entropy calculation methods to measure the level of new knowledge conveyed. The proposed metrics are applied to examine the information and readability levels of general books and specialized scientific journals across multiple disciplines. Contrary to expectations, it reveals that scientific articles today are neither more difficult to read nor more informative than everyday books from decades ago. These findings validate the longstanding criticism against current scientific publication trends and underscore the urgent need for a significant revision in research writing education.

In a wireless communication system with multiple users and relays, we explore the problem of minimizing the total transmission power while maintaining acceptable signal quality. This exploration focuses on wireless links that support the transmission of multiple data streams at once, using relays that amplify and forward signals. When applying this approach to a large number of relays, it becomes necessary to select the most suitable relays to reduce the complexity of the problem. By combining selection with resource allocation, we can achieve a more efficient use of available relays. However, this enlarged problem is too difficult to solve directly, so we develop two alternative optimization problems that use all relays but transmit either a single data stream or two data streams at once. In simulations, we find that transmitting two data streams achieves the highest level of security against eavesdroppers, providing a useful trade-off between the amount of power used and the level of security provided.

Two-dimensional systems with high electron mobility and topological properties, exemplified by quantum Hall and topological insulator materials, offer profound physical applications and are now possible to manipulate with graphene and other materials. These systems display robust edge currents, isolated in the bulk, which flow in both clockwise and counter-clockwise directions in time-reversal symmetry-broken topological insulators. This research explores a one-dimensional model consisting of multiple waveguides, where the edge current is confined within distinct channels and interacts with Fermi sea electrons through level and exchange couplings. Through numerical simulations, we observe the level current can function as a vector operator under electron spin flips, in contrast to the exchange current's analogous to a scalar operator. The competition between these two effects gives birth to level-induced Fermi sea magnetization. The model's versatility is demonstrated with various level placements and configurations, each yielding unique and intriguing outcomes. The results presented can be experimentally verified and may find applications in creating novel magnetic phases, stabilizing exotic states, and developing quantum Hall-based spin qubits with enhanced coherence.

Predictive control through model prediction reason (MPC) has been widely employed to regulate the operation of connected automated vehicles (CAVs). Nonetheless, most MPC frameworks fall short in incorporating safety-conscious constraints derived from the behavior of human-driven vehicles. To bridge this gap, we propose an MPC framework that integrates MPC-based human-driven vehicle predictions into the MPC objective function of CAVs through a weighted parameter. Furthermore, we introduce a novel MPC formulation that simultaneously minimizes travel time and adheres to safety constraints, ensuring the avoidance of collisions and adherence to stop lines. The proposed framework is validated through the development and operation of a CAV at a traffic signalized intersection, using the San Francisco Bay Area transit manager (SunTraffic) as a traffic simulation tool and the San Francisco Bay Traffic MPC (SFBT-MPC) controller to regulate CAV movement. The results, obtained from the the JAMSI CAV to the Bay Area Mutual Intelligent Surface (BAMIS) joint meeting in 2023, demonstrate the proposed model's effectiveness in balancing travel time and safety, based on the traffic signal timing and the behavior of human-driven vehicles.

Reinforcement learning mastering video games relies on fast agents capable of
acquiring high rewards quickly. Achieving similar success in learning text games
requires processing large amounts of text data, such as navigating millions of
states at one million steps per second. Existing state-space representations
fall short when interacting with primitive text game engines like TextWorld and
KiTheRGL, which can only manage around 20 steps per second. To overcome this
challenge, we introduce TextWorldExpress, an ultra-fast engine that utilizes
efficient token-tokenizations to speed up inferences while preserving semantic
clarity. TextWorldEnable enables seamless integration with original game files,
providing backward compatibility. Our experiments on various complex tasks
demonstrate these improvements yield up to 100-fold performance gains. We also
showcase the performance benefits of TextWorldExpress through integrations in
prominent research codes. The proposed solutions and the documentation are
available online under the MIT License.

Deep learning has achieved great success in various computer vision tasks, but it comes with high energy consumption that hinders its deployment on energy-constrained devices. To tackle this problem, we propose a novel approach called SE-LSTM, a method and hardware co-design framework for constructing energy-efficient deep neural networks that can classify videos. Our approach modifies the traditional long short-term memory (LSTM) architecture by integrating low-rank tensor decomposition techniques. This modification enables significant reduction of memory access counts by factorizing the weight matrices and adaptive gradient updates. As a result, our hardware design can achieve up to five times energy efficiency improvement over conventional GPUs. In experiments, SE-LSTM has demonstrated significant accuracy gains while maintaining the same energy budget that rivals the best-performing low-energy classifier in video recognition tasks.

When training neural networks, especially when training data is limited or when training occurs without supervision, leveraging large unsupervised corpora to enhance training is beneficial. Numerous techniques, including but not limited to projection, dropping, and embedding averaging, are utilized to incorporate the enhanced data. However, none of these approaches are optimized for a specific neural network architecture, data enhancement method, or training setting, resulting in confusion from the varied proposals in the literature. To clarify the situation, a unified framework is designed to systematically examine these data enhancement strategies under a specific neural network architecture. Our findings reveal that data enhancement strategies are beneficial in supervised learning scenarios with limited datasets. Additionally, they are found useful but also potentially redundant among themselves.

The notion of convexity in the gravity sector of a quantum field theory is analyzed, with a focus on its implied relationship to the feeble gravity conjecture. A mathematical framework for convexity in the gravity sector is established, and conditions for the persistence of convex functions under charged operator transformations are derived. The 2d conformal field theory model at a central charge value of $c=\bar c=1$ demonstrates an exponentially declining charge gap in contrast to its predicted quadratic behavior, indicating the insufficiency of the previously mentioned condition. Subsequently, specific operator conditions that could potentially violate the feeble gravity conjecture are investigated.

To investigate complex quantum systems, we have developed a new class of algorithms called the quantum imaginary duration evolution (QIDE) method, which allows us to study multiple interconnected regions of the system independently. By applying this method to models with piling up chaos, we were able to overcome a common limitation of the traditional infinite-time imaginary time evolution (ITGE) algorithm, where it tends to fail when dealing with models that have many interconnections. ITGE often results in an unmanageable level of disorder when trying to extend the simulation time. In contrast, our modified algorithm, M-QIDE, avoids this by not requiring the disentanglement of the entire system at once, instead entangling each individual region with its neighboring parts. Another benefit of the M-QIDE algorithm is its ability to preserve the overall particle distribution of the system, which is similar to the original system after imaginary time evolution. To show its effectiveness, we were able to achieve better results than the conventional Lanczos method in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency in our simulations of the Hubbard model.

This research paper proves that a local ring with a specific property, being F-pure, is associated with an infinite sequence of Frobenius linear rings. Furthermore, a new formula is derived for the tight Hilbert polynomial of this sequence. This formula has an application in determining the exact value of the tight Hilbert polynomial.

This paper outlines key principles for developing a supplementary services market, a crucial component of the electricity system that ensures stability. It offers guidance on regulatory frameworks and economic incentives to optimize the procurement of supplementary services, a complex process that involves maximizing the benefits of supplementary services while considering market dynamics. The author then introduces a game theory-based model to explore how market participants' actions influence the effectiveness of procurement mechanisms, ultimately affecting policy design. Furthermore, the author discusses potential research gaps in supplementary services markets and initiates a mathematical analysis using game theory, considering various procurement rules in market contexts that impact policy development.

In algebra, composing functions corresponds to adding elements in a group, while calculating their addition corresponds to composing the functions. Researchers are interested in determining the structure of a group based on the effects of repeatedly applying a single function based on the group's presentation. We establish a connection between the decomposition of functions into a composition of irreducible functions and the subgroup structure within a free group. Specifically, the decomposition into the minimum number of irreducible functions informs us about the indices of a sequence of subgroups and enables us to derive the composition factors. However, in a free group, we can't directly obtain the subgroups from the decompositions of irreducible functions. We establish a correspondence between the decomposition and iterates of compositions of words, allowing us to identify the index relationships. This leads to a new, innovative approach to the abstract solvability of the word problem.

This study investigates the detailed structure of the Standard Model's Higgs boson pair production through a specific decay channel, focusing on a one-dimensional phase space slicing method. By accurately calculating final state densities and applying this method to a complex process involving specific quark and boson combinations, it allows for a detailed examination of the process's topological structures and the impact of top quark decay correlations on cross-section estimates.

We can leverage the precision data from the $e^+e^-\to Zh$ and $\gamma\gamma$ processes at the Large Electron-Positron Collider (LEP) to place stringent constraints on new physics that could manifest through tree-level or loop-level interactions. Due to the sensitivity of the $\gamma\gamma$ channel to new heavy particles in the loop, it is particularly useful for detecting new physics that does not directly interact with the Standard Model at a tree level. Using the full LEP data set, we conducted an in-depth analysis of $e^+e^-\to Zh$ and $\gamma\gamma$ processes to set new limits on the parameters of the Standard Model and various two-Higgs-doublet models, specifically in the "aligned limit" and "type-II" variant. Our analysis shows that LEP data severely restrict the parameter space of the aligned model, particularly for scenarios where $\sin(\alpha/\beta)\approx 0$ and $0 < m_H \lesssim 110$ GeV. On the other hand, the type-II model requires $m_H \gtrsim 115$ GeV, which is consistent with the LEP findings for the decoupling regime.

Saturn's northern atmosphere is characterized by the development of planetary polar vortexes that follow the seasonal changes, transitioning from the summer hemisphere to the winter one, a process taking approximately three Earth years. During the last observed period, the polar polar vortex was forming a hexagonal structure in the summer northern atmosphere. Now, our new analysis of data from the Cassini mission reveals the formation of a large summer polar vortex just outside the famous hexagon. Within half an Earth year, this vortex adopts a distinct shape resembling the Mediterranean Sea's coastline, featuring a prominent cape in its eastern section. The emergence of this vortex signifies the approaching transition of Saturn's seasons, where the southern polar region will soon begin developing its own polar polar vortex.

For a specific set of parameters, a solution is found that meets the criteria for a solution outside a convex obstacle in the exterior of the domain, where the solution exponentially decays as the distance increases. Building on previous research by Cuccheccanti-Monticelli and Druet, this study introduces a new method using an exponentially modified linear equation to directly construct a solution, improving upon an existing exponential bound found by Cuccheccanti-Monticelli-Montaruli.

We demonstrate how the technique of local- and semi-parametric-witnessing in characteristic zero can be adapted to implement similar methods in positive characteristic. Specifically, given a definable variety over the field of characteristic zero with parameters from the base field, our modification of the characteristic zero deduction yields a local- or semi-parametric identity involving those same parameters. This characteristic zero identity can then be utilized to establish the existence of analogous witnesses in fields of high enough characteristic. These witnesses facilitate isomorphisms between respective characteristic zero and positive characteristic instances, thereby enabling the establishment of the positive-characteristic semi-parametric local-Uniform Completeness Theorem.

V$_2$O$_3$ films that have been grown on the (0001) surface are an ideal system for studying the metal-insulator transition because of their minimal distortion.  V$_2$O$_3$ films and their surface layers exhibit different electrical properties; while the bulk remains insulating, the few monolayers near the surface behave as a conductor.  To understand the cause of this metal-insulator transition, we did resistivity measurements at room temperature and in a cryogenic temperature, in addition to taking XPS spectra of V$_2$O$_3$ samples with H- and O-terminations.  Our结果显示，the metal-insulator transition is closely tied to the surface termination type, as applied an external electric field can switch the temperature at which the transition occurs.

Using two bosonic pairs in distinct internal states within one-dimensional traps, we have analyzed the transition from stability to instability in quantum states. By applying a precise method for quantum non-interacting particles, we can observe how weak repulsion gradually increases until it forms double dark-rogue states, causing a sudden collapse. Our study shows that as the trap size shrinks, the point at which condensation occurs quickly rises, even for nearly interacting particles. Notably, there is a pivotal moment when the system transitions from stability to double darkness, allowing us to derive an almost precise formula for how the critical density scales in relation to repulsive strength and trap density.
We establish the polarization of homogenized free ternary collections and provide a preliminary investigation into normalized binary and quaternary free collections.

Let G be a connected reductive algebraic group defined over the real numbers. Let me denote the set of conjugacy classes under the action of G(R) on its own group elements. For any Borel subset O of G(R)/G,R, we can associate a number denoted as om(O), which represents a measure of O. The focus of this article is on establishing certain formulas to adjust the measure of the set of elements in G(R) whose orbits match a specific conjugacy class within G, up to a certain growth factor as we modify some algebraic parameters. These adjustments are particularly useful in modifying the local factors employed in formulating conjectures connecting the analytic values of L-functions to the spectral and discrete sides of a generating series.

To study how light affects complex molecular structures, we propose using X-ray pulses and proposing a method to analyze their dynamics. This method involves using high-energy spectral data from X-rays that have scattered off a substance. We demonstrate that this approach can accurately retrieve the detailed structure (electron distribution) of atoms and even smaller units (individual atoms' nuclear positions) from their oscillations, even when the X-ray data is not very high quality. The success of this method relies on using X-ray pulses whose frequencies match the natural vibrations of atoms, significantly outperforming a previous technique based on scattering patterns.

By applying a类比 to the Ising model of disordered classical spins, we analyzed complex quantum error correction circuits that use the 3D cat code, taking into account various disorder patterns. Our findings reveal that to maintain a high error correction effect in the presence of disorder, the initial state must be located in the most centrally concentrated region of the circuit's effective boundary. Moreover, we've identified the most effective geometric configurations for the code's logical information. This analysis can be applied to the design of more efficient quantum memory circuits.

Recent theoretical predictions have identified a new class of stable vanadium-based materials on the Te- honeycomb lattice, offering an attractive platform for two-dimensional quantum states. In this study, we examine multiple Te2V monolayer models and investigate the impact of structural factors, magnetic properties, and potential fluctuations on their electronic behavior. Examinations are conducted utilizing first-principles calculations and tight-binding models. We observe that Te2V monolayers with specific packing arrangements exhibit large-gap electronic behavior. Notably, these materials display robust two-dimensional anomalous Hall effects induced by time-reversal symmetry breaking when the Te atom is substituted with a magnetic variant. It is proven through both numerical and theoretical reasoning that flattened edge anomalies exist in both neutral and doped Te2V monolayers, resulting in robust topological conductivity. The presence of Te orbitals within the gap induces significant size insulation regardless of disorder strength. The presence of out-of-plane spin texture provides anomalous edge fluctuations in response to light-generated chirality. Our studies reveal that the Te2V material system, particularly doped Te2V, exhibits robust and customizable two-dimensional anomalous topological conducting behavior.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element method to model single-phase Darcy flow in a fractured porous medium, where the matrix domain is partitioned by a set of non-overlapping fractures with given permeability properties. Our approach involves discretizing the matrix domain using standard simplicial elements and the fractures using surface elements of lower dimension. We employ specific approximation schemes for the pressure and velocity fields in both the matrix and fractures, and we demonstrate convergence towards the exact solution under certain conditions of fracture distribution. Furthermore, our method can be efficiently solved through decentralized algorithms due to the limited coupling between fractures.

To develop high-performance spin switches, a novel multilayer structure is proposed consisting of two distinct magnetic layers with opposite magnetizations and an intermediate nonmagnetic channel featuring unique electronic behavior. The incorporation of a homochiral ferromagnetic layer, exhibiting magnetic anisotropy and unique magnetic spin arrangement, significantly enhances the device's sensitivity to magnetization changes. This proposed design exhibits a substantial reduction in resistance when one magnetic layer aligns with the other, and opposes it when there's a net change in magnetization.
